The lām is attached (mutaʿalliq) to the omitted khabar whose place it has taken, just as the bāʾ was in بِسم الله; its implied form is "الْحَمد ثَابت لله" (praise is established for Allah), or "مُسْتَقر" (settled), and the like.

The accusative of رب الْعَالمين is permitted as a vocative, or as praise (al-madḥ); its nominative is also permitted on the reading "هُوَ رب الْعَالمين" (He is the Lord of the worlds). ملك يَوْم الدّين is likewise like it. يَوْم الدّين is an adverb (ẓarf) treated as an object by extension (ʿalā al-saʿa); that is why ملك is made muḍāf to it (genitive construct). The same holds in the reading of whoever read مَالك with alif. As for whoever reads مَالك, a direct object must be assumed to be omitted, its implied form being "مَالك يَوْم الدّين الْفَصْل وَالْقَضَاء" (Master, on the Day of Judgement, of the decision and the judgement) and the like, because it is transitive. [Translator's note: the two readings are written identically in the edition; the second is presumably the reading treated as an active participle taking an object, as opposed to the first treated as a genitive construct.]

The plural of مَالك is ملاك and ملك; the plural of ملك is أَمْلَاك and ملوك. Abū ʿAmr read ملك with the lām made vowelless, just as one says فَخذ and فخذ; its plural on this view is أملك and ملوك. The accusative is also permitted in ملك as a ḥāl (circumstantial), or as a vocative, or as praise, or as a naʿt (adjective) of رب in the view of whoever puts it in the accusative.

We only mention these aspects so that the workings of i'rab and its analogical measures may be known, not so that it may be recited thus; for it is not permitted to recite except by what has been transmitted and authenticated from the well-known trustworthy authorities, from the Companions and the Successors, may Allah be pleased with them, and agrees with the script of the Muṣḥaf.

mekki-muskil:5-5.t:
The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: {إياك نعْبد}. ايا, according to al-Khalīl and others, is a pronoun (ism muḍmar) made muḍāf (genitive construct) to the kāf; this is anomalous (shādhdh), as no other pronoun is known to have been made muḍāf. Ibn Kaysān reported that the kāf is the noun, and ايا was brought in so that the kāf could lean on it, since it cannot stand by itself. Al-Mubarrad said: ايا is a vague noun (ism mubham) made muḍāf for specification; yet no other indeclinable vague noun is known to have been made muḍāf, and it is a principle of the vague noun that when it is made muḍāf it is indefinite and declinable, as with غير, بعض and كل. The Kufans said: إياك as a whole is a pronoun; yet no other pronoun is known whose ending changes, so that you say in it إِيَّاه, إِيَّاهَا and إِيَّاكُم. It is accusative by نعبد, a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) placed first; had it come later it would not be detached but would become an attached kāf, and you would say نعبدك.

His words {نستعين}: its pattern is نستفعل and its original form is نستعون, because it is from العون (help). The vowel of the wāw was cast onto the ʿayn, so the ʿayn took kasra and the wāw became vowelless, and it turned into yāʾ because of the kasra before it, since in the speech of the Arabs there is no vowelless wāw preceded by kasra, nor a vowelless yāʾ preceded by ḍamma. It was only weakened because the past tense is weakened. The maṣdar (verbal noun) is استعانة, originally استعوان: the vowel of the wāw was cast onto the ʿayn, the wāw was turned into alif, and one of the two alifs was dropped because of the meeting of two vowelless letters — some say the first, some say the second — and the hāʾ (tāʾ marbūṭa) was added in compensation for what was dropped. It is permitted to give kasra to the nūn, the tāʾ and the alif at the beginning of this verb and of its like outside the Quran; that is not good with the yāʾ.

His words, Majestic and Exalted: {اهدنا} is a request and petition; it is treated in i'rab like the imperative. However, it is indeclinable (mabnī) according to the Basrans, the dropping of the yāʾ from it being indeclinability, and declinable according to the Kufans, the dropping of the yāʾ from it being the jussive. The alif is a connective alif (alif al-waṣl), given kasra at the beginning of speech because it and what follows it are vowelless, since it was brought in only so that speech may begin with it and has no share of the vowels. It is also said that it was given kasra because of the kasra of the third letter. It was not given ḍamma because of the heaviness of moving from ḍamma to kasra, and it was not given fatḥa so that it would not resemble the alif of the first person. This is the reason for the connective alif wherever it occurs in verbs and nouns. If the third letter of the verb has ḍamma, the alif takes ḍamma by assimilation (itbāʿ): its vowel is for the meeting of two vowelless letters, and ḍamma was chosen because the third letter has ḍamma, as in ادخل and اخْرُج. As for the connective alif that comes with the lām of definiteness, in الرجل and الْغُلَام, it takes fatḥa at the beginning of speech to distinguish its entering on verbs and nouns from its entering on particles. اهدنا takes two objects, and it is permitted to confine it to one of them; here they are نَا and الصِّرَاط.

mekki-muskil:6-6.t: His words {الْمُسْتَقيم}: its original form is المستقوم, and its weakening (iʿlāl) in the noun and the maṣdar (verbal noun) is like the weakening of نستعين.

mekki-muskil:7-7.t:
His words {صِرَاط الَّذين} is a badal (substitute) for the first الصِّرَاط. الَّذين is a vague (mubham), indeclinable (mabnī), incomplete noun that requires a ṣila (relative clause) and a resumptive pronoun (ʿāʾid). It is not declined in the singular and the plural, but it is declined in the dual because the dual is sound, since it does not vary and occurs across all nouns in only one pattern; the plural is not like that. The reason for the indeclinability of الَّذِي is that it resembles the particles through its vagueness and its applying to everything, so it was denied case-inflection just as the particles are denied it. It is also said that it was made indeclinable only because it is incomplete and requires a ṣila, so it is like part of a noun, and part of a noun is always indeclinable, since case-inflection only occurs at the ends of nouns and verbs. It has also been said that الَّذين is a noun of plurality (ism jamʿ) and not a plural.

The singular of الَّذين is لذ, like عم and شج. When the alif and lām entered it and became permanent, the yāʾ returned, as it returns in قَاض, so you said الَّذِي. Its original form is to be written with two lāms, but they dropped one of the two lāms because of frequent usage, for lightness, and the plural followed the singular since it is indeclinable like it, being closer to it in case-inflection; the dual was written with two lāms according to the original.

The ṣila of الَّذين is His words أَنْعَمت عَلَيْهِم, and the hāʾ and mīm (the pronoun) refer back to them.

His words {غير المغضوب عَلَيْهِم}: غير is a vague noun, except that it is declined because it is constantly muḍāf (in genitive construct). Its genitive is as a badal for الَّذين, or as a naʿt (adjective) of them, since they are not meant as specific individuals, so they are treated like an indefinite noun, and thus غير may be a naʿt for them. It is a principle of غير that it is indefinite even if it is made muḍāf to a definite noun, because it does not denote a specific thing. The accusative of غير has been transmitted from Ibn Kathīr and others; its accusative is as a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the hāʾ and mīm in عَلَيْهِم, or from الَّذين, since their form is that of a definite noun. If you wish, you may make it accusative as a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ) according to the Basrans, though the Kufans disallowed it because of the entry of لَا. And if you wish, you may make it accusative by an implied أَعنِي (I mean).

The second عَلَيْهِم is in the position of the nominative as the deputy agent (mafʿūl lam yusamma fāʿiluhu, i.e. nāʾib fāʿil) of المغضوب, because it means "those with whom [He] is angry". There is no pronoun in it, since it is only made transitive by a preposition, like مر بزيد (he passed by Zayd); that is why it was not put in the plural.

His words {وَلَا الضَّالّين}: لَا is redundant (zāʾida) for emphasis according to the Basrans, and in the sense of غير according to the Kufans. Among the Arabs are those who replace the vowelless letter that precedes a doubled letter with a hamza, saying وَلَا الضألّين; that is when it is an alif. Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī read thus. He wanted to give the alif a vowel because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, but it could not be given a vowel, so he replaced it with a letter akin to it, close to it in point of articulation, sturdier and stronger than it, namely the hamza. [Translator's note: the edition prints the hamzated form identically to the ordinary form, وَلَا الضَّالّين; the hamzated form الضألّين is evidently intended.]

muyesser-irab:1-1.t:
﴿بسم﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted [verb], its implied form being "I begin" (أبتدئ), so the preposition and its genitive noun are in the position of an accusative (manṣūb) fronted mafʿūl bihi (direct object); or [its implied form being] "my beginning" (ابتدائي), so the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to an omitted khabar (predicate) of an omitted mubtadaʾ (subject).
﴿الله﴾: the Name of Majesty, muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct).
﴿الرحمن الرحيم﴾: two naʿts (adjectives) of Allah the Exalted; the clause of the basmala is initial (ibtidāʾiyya), a clause with no grammatical position.

muyesser-irab:2-2.t:
﴿الحمد﴾: mubtadaʾ (subject).
﴿لله﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted khabar (predicate).
﴿رب﴾: a naʿt (adjective) of «لله», or a badal (substitute) from it.
﴿العالمين﴾: muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), genitive (majrūr), the sign of its genitive being the yāʾ in place of the kasra, because it is treated like the sound masculine plural.

muyesser-irab:3-3.t: ﴿الرحمن الرحيم﴾: two naʿts (adjectives) of Allah the Exalted as well.

muyesser-irab:4-4.t:
﴿مالك﴾: a fourth naʿt (adjective) of Allah.
﴿يوم الدين﴾: muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct).

muyesser-irab:5-5.t:
﴿إياك﴾: a detached pronoun in the position of an accusative (manṣūb), a fronted mafʿūl bihi (direct object), [fronted] for restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ).
﴿نعبد﴾: an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ); its fāʿil (agent) is a pronoun necessarily latent (mustatir) in it, its implied form being "we" (نحن).
﴿وإياك نستعين﴾: conjoined to «إياك نعبد»; «نستعين»: an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ); its fāʿil (agent) is a pronoun necessarily latent (mustatir) in it, its implied form being "we" (نحن).

muyesser-irab:6-6.t:
﴿اهدنا﴾: a verb of supplication, indeclinable (mabnī) on the omission of the weak [letter] (حذف العلة) [Translator's note: the source reads «حذف العلة», presumably for «حذف حرف العلة», "the omission of the weak letter"]; «نا» is an attached pronoun in the position of an accusative (manṣūb), mafʿūl bihi (direct object); its fāʿil (agent) is a pronoun necessarily latent (mustatir) in it, its implied form being "you" (أنت).
﴿الصراط﴾: a second mafʿūl bihi (direct object), or accusative by removal of the preposition (manṣūb bi-nazʿ al-khāfiḍ), because «هدى» is transitive only to one object, and is made transitive to the second by lām or by «إلى».
﴿المستقيم﴾: a naʿt (adjective) of «الصراط».

muyesser-irab:7-7.t:
﴿صراط﴾: a badal (substitute) of full correspondence (badal muṭābiq) from «الصراط».
﴿الذين﴾: a relative noun, muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), in the position of a genitive (majrūr).
﴿أنعمت﴾: a past verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on sukūn because of its attachment to a vowelled nominative pronoun; the tāʾ is an attached pronoun in the position of a nominative (marfūʿ), fāʿil (agent); the clause «أنعمت» is a clause with no grammatical position, because it is the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative noun.
﴿عليهم﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) «أنعمت».
﴿غير﴾: a badal (substitute) from the pronoun in «عليهم», or from «الذين», or a naʿt (adjective) of «الذين».
﴿المغضوب﴾: muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct).
﴿عليهم﴾: a preposition and its genitive noun in the position of a nominative (marfūʿ), nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) of «المغضوب», because it is a passive participle.
﴿ولا﴾: the wāw is a conjunction, and «لا» is a connective (ṣila) to emphasise the meaning of negation, namely the meaning of negation contained in «غير».
﴿الضالين﴾: conjoined (maʿṭūf) to «المغضوب عليهم», genitive (majrūr), the sign of its genitive being the yāʾ, because it is a sound masculine plural.

nahhas-irab:1-1.t:
(اسم) is in the genitive (makhfūḍ) through the redundant (zāʾida) bāʾ. Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] said: The bāʾ was given kasra to distinguish between what makes a noun genitive while being only a particle and nothing else, and what makes a noun genitive while it may sometimes be a noun, such as the kāf. It may be asked: why did the bāʾ come to make nouns genitive? The answer to this, and for all the genitive-governing particles, is that these particles have no meaning except in nouns, and they do not resemble verbs so as to govern as verbs govern; so they were given what occurs only in nouns, namely the genitive (khafḍ) — the early Basrans call it jarr. The position of the bāʾ and what follows it is, according to al-Farrāʾ, accusative, in the sense of "I began with «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم»" or "I begin with «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم»"; according to the Basrans it is nominative, in the sense of "my beginning is with the name of Allah". ʿAlī ibn Ḥamza al-Kisāʾī said:
The bāʾ has no grammatical position, and the "passing" falls upon something unspecified when you say: مررت بزيد ("I passed by Zayd").
The alif in «اسم» is a connecting alif (alif waṣl), because you say سُمَيّ (in the diminutive); for this reason it is dropped in pronunciation. As for its being dropped in writing, there are four views: al-Farrāʾ said it is because of frequent use; it is also reported [that it was dropped] because the bāʾ is never written separately; al-Akhfash Saʿīd said it was dropped because it is not part of the pronunciation; and the fourth view is that the original form is سِم and سُم. Abū Zayd recited: [al-Rajaz metre]
1-
بسم الذي في كلّ سورة سمه
(In the name of the One whose name is in every sura.)
— also with ḍamma, so that the original would be سما; then you brought the bāʾ and it became بسم, then the kasra was dropped and it became بسم. On this view there was never an alif in it at all. [Translator's note: the text as printed reads «ثم حذفت الكسرة فصار بسم» ("then the kasra was dropped and it became بسم"); the vowelling needed to follow the argument (presumably بِسِم → بِسْم) has been lost in the source.] The original pattern of اسم is fiʿl; it can only be that, for a reason that requires it. Its plural is أسماء, and the plural of أسماء is أسامي. You made اسم muḍāf (in a genitive construct) to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; the alif in "Allah" is a connecting alif according to those who say the original is لاه. Some of the Arabs make it a disjunctive alif (alif qaṭʿ) and say بسم الله [pronouncing the hamza], because it always accompanies the word, like a disjunctive alif.
«الرَّحْمنِ» is a naʿt (adjective) of Allah the Exalted. It is not put in the dual or plural, because it is used only of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The lām is assimilated into the rāʾ because of their closeness and because the lām of definiteness is so frequent.
«الرَّحِيمِ» is also a naʿt; its plural is رحماء. This [form] is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, Banū Asad, Qays and Rabīʿa; Banū Tamīm say رِحيم, رِغيف, بِعير [with kasra on the first letter]. [Translator's note: the printed text shows these words without vowelling; the Tamīmī kasra on the first letter is the well-known feature intended.] In pausing you may give the kasra a trace (ishmām) or make it quiescent; quiescence is better with what has kasra, and ishmām is more common with what has ḍamma.
The accusative is permissible in «الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ» as praise (madḥ), and the nominative by implying a mubtadaʾ (subject); it is also permissible to make the first genitive and the second nominative, or to make one of them nominative and the other accusative.

nahhas-irab:2-2.t:
«الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ»: [الحمد] is nominative by being the mubtadaʾ (subject) according to the view of the Basrans. Al-Kisāʾī said: «الحمد» is nominative through the pronoun that is in the "ṣifa", the ṣifa being the lām — he treated the lām like a verb. Al-Farrāʾ said:
«الحمد» is nominative through the "maḥall", which is the lām — he treated the lām like a noun, because it cannot stand by itself. Al-Kisāʾī calls the genitive-governing particles ṣifāt ("qualifiers"), al-Farrāʾ calls them maḥāll ("places"), and the Basrans call them ẓurūf ("adverbials/containers"). Ibn ʿUyayna and Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj read «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» as a maṣdar (verbal noun) [i.e. in the accusative, الحمدَ لله], and this is the dialect of Qays and al-Ḥārith ibn Sāma. [Translator's note: the source prints the standard vowelling «الْحَمْدُ» here although it describes the accusative reading; likewise in the variant readings below, the printed Quranic text does not show the variant vowels being described.] The nominative is better both in wording and in meaning. As for wording: because it is a definite noun about which you have predicated. As for meaning: if you use the nominative you are stating that your praise and the praise of others belongs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic; if you use the accusative, it does not go beyond your own praise. Al-Farrāʾ reported: «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» and «الحمد لله» [i.e. الحمدِ لِلّه and الحمدُ لُلّه].
Abū Jaʿfar said: I heard ʿAlī ibn Sulaymān [al-Akhfash the Younger] say: neither of these two is permissible according to the Basrans. Abū Jaʿfar said: These are two known dialects and two existing readings, and each has a rationale. Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAyyāsh related from Zurayq from al-Ḥasan that he read «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» [i.e. الحمدِ لِلّه], and Ibrāhīm ibn Abī ʿAbla read «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» [i.e. الحمدُ لُلّه]; this is the dialect of some of Banū Rabīʿa, and the kasra is the dialect of Tamīm. As for the dialect with kasra: this phrase is very frequent in people's speech, and ḍamma is heavy, especially when a kasra follows it; so they replaced the ḍamma with kasra and treated the two as a single thing — kasra with kasra is lighter, and likewise ḍamma with ḍamma; that is why «الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ» was said [in these two ways].
«لِلَّهِ» is genitive through the lām, which is zāʾida (redundant). [Translator's note: the source says «باللام الزائدة»; the lām here is not normally classed as redundant, but it is translated as written.] Sībawayh held that the original vowel of the lām is fatḥa; what shows you this is that when you use a pronoun you say الحمد لَهُ, returning it to its origin; it was given kasra only with an overt noun, to distinguish between the lām of the genitive and the lām of emphasis (tawkīd).
«رَبِّ» is genitive as a naʿt (adjective) of Allah. «الْعالَمِينَ» is genitive by the iḍāfa (genitive construct); the sign of the genitive is the yāʾ, because it is of the same kind as kasra. The nūn, according to Sībawayh, is as it were a compensation for the vowel and the tanwīn that were withheld; according to Abū al-ʿAbbās [al-Mubarrad] the nūn is a compensation for the tanwīn; and according to Abū Isḥāq [al-Zajjāj] a compensation for the vowel. It was given fatḥa to distinguish it from the nūn of the dual. Al-Kisāʾī said: «رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ» is permissible [in the accusative, ربَّ العالمين], as you say:
الحمد لله ربًّا وإلهًا ("praise be to Allah as Lord and God"), i.e. as a ḥāl (circumstantial). Abū Ḥātim said: the accusative is in the sense of "I praise Allah, the Lord of the worlds". Abū Isḥāq said: the accusative is permissible as a vocative (nidāʾ) in construct. Abū al-Ḥasan ibn Kaysān said: the accusative as a vocative in construct is far-fetched, because it would make it two separate utterances; rather it is accusative as praise (madḥ). The nominative is also permissible, i.e. "He is the Lord of the worlds". Abū Jaʿfar said: We mentioned in the earlier book that, for intensiveness, one says ربّاه, ربّه and ربّته. Its explanation is that the original is ربّبه, then a yāʾ is substituted for the bāʾ, as one says:
قصّيت أظفاري and تقصّيت [from قصّصت, "I clipped my nails"], then a tāʾ is substituted for the yāʾ, just as it is substituted for the wāw in تالله.

nahhas-irab:3-4.t:
«الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ» is permissible [in the accusative] as praise (madḥ); it is permissible to make both nominative by implying a mubtadaʾ (subject); it is permissible to make one of them nominative and the other accusative; and it is permissible to make the first genitive and the second nominative or accusative.
Muḥammad ibn al-Samayfaʿ al-Yamānī read «مالك يوم الدّين» with مالك in the accusative. There are four dialectal forms of it: مالِك, مَلِك, مَلْك and مَلِيك, as Labīd said: [al-Kāmil metre] 2-
فاقنع بما قسم المليك فإنّما ... قسم المعايش بيننا علّامها
(Be content with what the Sovereign has apportioned, for the One who apportioned livelihoods among us is the One who knows them best.)
In terms of Arabic [grammar] there are twenty-five ways [of reading] it: one says «ملك يوم الدين» as a naʿt (adjective); in the nominative by implying a mubtadaʾ; in the accusative as praise, as a vocative, as a ḥāl (circumstantial), and as a naʿt according to the reading of those who read «رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ» [in the accusative]. These are six ways; «مالك» has the same, «مَلْك» has the same, and «مليك» has the same. That makes twenty-four. The twenty-fifth is reported from Abū Ḥaywa Shurayḥ ibn Yazīd, that he read «ملك يوم الدّين», and it is also reported from him that he read «ملك يوم الدين». [Translator's note: the vowelling that distinguishes these two reported readings is missing from the source; in other works Abū Ḥaywa is credited with the verbal reading مَلَكَ يومَ الدين.] Abū Jaʿfar said: the plural of مالك is مُلّاك and مُلَّك; the plural of مَلِك is أملاك and ملوك; and the plural of مَلْك is أَمْلُك and ملوك — this on the view of those who say «مَلْك» is a dialectal form and not a quiescent-ised form of مَلِك. The plural of مليك is مُلَكاء.
«يَوْمِ» is genitive by مالك being put in construct with it, and «الدِّينِ» is genitive by يوم being put in construct with it. The plural of يوم is أيّام; the original is أَيْوام: the wāw was assimilated into the yāʾ. No verb is used from it.
Sībawayh held that if a verb were used from it, one would say يُمْتُ. The plural of الدين is أديان and ديون.

nahhas-irab:5-5.t:
«إِيَّاكَ» is accusative because «نَعْبُدُ» falls upon it [as its object]. Al-Faḍl ibn ʿĪsā al-Raqāshī read «إِيَّاكَ» with fatḥa on the hamza [أَيّاك], and ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid read «إِيَّاكَ» without shadda [إِياك]. [Translator's note: the source prints the standard form in both cases; the variants are as described in the words.] The noun in إيّاك, according to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh, is إيّا, and the kāf is in the position of the genitive; according to the Kufans, إيّاك in its entirety is the noun. Al-Khalīl, may Allah have mercy on him, held that it is a pronoun noun. Abū al-ʿAbbās said: this is a mistake — a pronoun is not put in construct; rather it is a vague noun (mubham) like «كلّ», put in construct with what follows it.
«نَعْبُدُ» is an imperfect verb (fiʿl mustaqbal); it is nominative according to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh because of its resemblance to nouns. Al-Kisāʾī said: the imperfect verb is nominative through the added letters at its beginning. Al-Farrāʾ said: it is nominative through its being free from the jussive- and subjunctive-governing particles.
The [second] «إِيَّاكَ» is accusative through «نستعين» — a clause conjoined to a clause. Yaḥyā ibn Waththāb and al-Aʿmash read «نَسْتَعِينُ» with kasra on the nūn [نِستعين], and this is the dialect of Tamīm, Asad, Qays and Rabīʿa. They did this to show that it is from استعون يستعين. The original of «نستعين» is نستعوِن: the vowel of the wāw was transferred to the ʿayn, and when what precedes the wāw had kasra it became a yāʾ. The maṣdar (verbal noun) is استعانة, the original being استعوان: the vowel of the wāw was transferred to the ʿayn, and when what precedes the wāw had fatḥa it became an alif. Two quiescent letters cannot meet, so the second alif was dropped because it is the augment — and it is said [rather] the first, because the second carries a meaning — and the hāʾ [tāʾ marbūṭa] was made obligatory as a compensation.

nahhas-irab:6-6.t:
«إِنَّا هُدْنا» [Translator's note: so printed in the source; the word under discussion is clearly «اهْدِنَا» of verse 6, and the heading appears to be a transcription error.] — it is a supplication and a request; according to al-Farrāʾ it is in the position of the jussive (jazm), and according to the Basrans it is in a state of pause (waqf) [i.e. indeclinable], and for that reason the yāʾ was dropped. The alif is a connecting alif (alif waṣl), because the first letter of the imperfect has fatḥa; you gave it kasra because it is from يهدي. The nūn and alif are the first mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and «الصِّراطَ» is the second object. Its plural of paucity is أَصْرِطة and its plural of abundance is صُرُط. Al-Akhfash said: the people of the Hijaz treat الصراط as feminine. Ibn ʿAbbās read «السراط» with sīn, and some of Qays pronounce it between ṣād and zāy; it is not permissible to make it a [pure] zāy unless it is quiescent. Quṭrub said: if, after the sīn within the same word, there is a ṭāʾ, a qāf, a khāʾ or a ghayn, you may change it into a ṣād.
«الْمُسْتَقِيمَ» is a naʿt (adjective) of الصراط.

nahhas-irab:7-7.t:
«صِراطَ الَّذِينَ»: [صراط] is a badal (substitute). «الَّذِينَ» is in the position of the genitive by the iḍāfa (genitive construct); it is indeclinable (mabnī) so that a noun is not declined from its middle. «أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ» is part of the ṣila (relative clause), and the hāʾ and mīm refer back to الذين. In «عليهم» there are five dialectal forms, all of which have been read. Ibn Abī Isḥāq read «أنعمت عليهُمُو» with ḍamma on the hāʾ and the wāw retained; this is the original, that the wāw be retained just as the alif is retained in the dual. Al-Ḥasan read «أنعمت عليهِمِي» with kasra on the hāʾ and the yāʾ retained: he gave the hāʾ kasra because he disliked combining a yāʾ and a ḍamma, the hāʾ being no strong barrier, and he substituted yāʾ for the wāw because what preceded it had kasra. The people of Medina read «عَلَيْهِمْ» with kasra on the hāʾ and the mīm quiescent; this is the dialect of the people of Najd. Ḥamza and the people of Kufa read «عَلَيْهُمْ» with ḍamma on the hāʾ and the mīm quiescent; they dropped the wāw because of its heaviness, and because the meaning is not ambiguous since in the dual one says عليهما. The fifth form was read by al-Aʿraj: «عليهِمُو» with kasra on the hāʾ and [ḍamma before] the wāw. [Translator's note: the source says «بكسر الهاء والواو», literally "with kasra of the hāʾ and the wāw"; translated as written, with the intended form supplied in brackets.] Two anomalous forms are also reported: ḍamma on both the hāʾ and the mīm without wāw, and kasra on both without yāʾ. [Translator's note: the source reads «لغتنا», evidently for «لغتان», "two dialectal forms".] Muḥammad ibn Yazīd [al-Mubarrad] said: this is not permissible, because it is mustaqbal [Translator's note: so in the source; the word seems corrupt — perhaps «مستثقل», "felt to be heavy"]. If it is asked: why then is منهُ said, with ḍamma on the hāʾ? The answer is that the nūn in «منه» is quiescent. Abū al-ʿAbbās said: some people of Banū Bakr ibn Wāʾil say عليكِم, giving the kāf kasra just as they give the hāʾ kasra, because it is a voiceless (mahmūsa) letter like it, and it is a pronoun just as the hāʾ is a pronoun. This is a gross error, because it is not like it in faintness.
«غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ» is genitive as a badal (substitute) from الذين, or, if you wish, as a naʿt (adjective). Ibn Kaysān said: it may also be a badal from the hāʾ and mīm in عليهم. Al-Khalīl, may Allah have mercy on him, related from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr «غَيْرَ الْمَغْضُوبِ» in the accusative. Al-Akhfash said: it is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), or, if you wish, as an exception (istithnāʾ). Abū al-ʿAbbās said: it is an exception not of the same kind as what precedes (istithnāʾ laysa min al-awwal). The Kufans said: it cannot be an exception, because «ولا» comes after it, and «لا» is not added in exception. Abū Jaʿfar said: this does not follow, because it carries the meaning of negation. He said «غير المغضوب عليهم» and did not say "المغضوبين" because there is no pronoun in it. Ibn Kaysān said: it is singular with a plural meaning, and so is every passive participle when it has no nominative pronoun [Translator's note: the source reads «إذا لم يكن فيه خفض مرفوع», literally "when it has no nominative genitive"; the wording seems disturbed and is rendered by sense], such as المنظور إليهم and المرغوب فيهم. «الْمَغْضُوبِ» [is genitive] by غير being put in construct with it, and «عَلَيْهِمْ» is in the position of the nominative because it is the noun whose agent is not named [i.e. the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent)].
«وَلَا» is zāʾida (redundant) according to the Basrans and in the sense of غير according to the Kufans. «الضَّالِّينَ» is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to «المغضوب عليهم»; the Kufans call this nasq, and Sībawayh calls it ishrāk ("association"). The original of الضالّين is الضاللين; then the lām was assimilated into the lām, so two quiescent letters met, and this was allowed because the alif has prolongation and the second is assimilated. However, Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī used a hamza and read «وَلَا الضَّأْلِّينَ».

nahhas-meani:1-1.t:
Among what we set out to treat is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿بِسْمِ ٱللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيـمِ﴾
Most of the Basrans said: The meaning is: "The first thing with which I begin is "بسم اللهِ", and the first of my speech is "بِسمِ اللهِ"."
Sībawayh said: The meaning of the bāʾ is ilṣāq (attachment/adhesion).
Al-Farrāʾ said: The position of the bāʾ is accusative (manṣūb), and the meaning is: "I have begun with the name of Allah," and "I begin with the name of Allah."
Concerning the derivation of "اسم" there are two views:
One of them: it is from al-sumuww, which is elevation and height; it was called "اسم" because its bearer is, as it were, raised up by it.
And it was said: it is from wasamtu (I marked); it was called "اسم" because it is to its bearer like a mark (sima), i.e. he is known by it.
The second view is mistaken, because what has dropped from it is its lām (final radical), so it is established that it is from samā yasmū.
Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā said: One says sim and sam, and one says ism with a kasra on the alif, and one says it with a ḍamma.
Whoever puts a ḍamma on the alif takes it from samawtu asmū.
And whoever puts a kasra takes it from samaytu asmī.
Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ said: The meaning of "بسمِ اللهِ" is "in the name of al-ilāh (the deity)"; they dropped the hamza and assimilated the first lām into the second, so it became a doubled lām, just as He, Majestic and Mighty, said: ﴿لَّٰكِنَّاْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ رَبِّي﴾, whose meaning is: "لَكِنْ أَنَا هُوَ اللهُ رَبِّي"; that is how al-Ḥasan read it.
Sībawayh has two views on this:
One of them: that the origin is ilāh, then the alif and lām were brought in as a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the hamza; likewise al-nās, in his view, has the origin unās.
The other view — which is also the view of his followers — is that the origin is lāh, then the alif and lām entered upon it; and they cited:
لاَهِ ابنُ عَمِّكَ لاَ أَفْضَلْتَ فِي حَسَبٍ * عَنِّي وَلاَ أَنْتَ دَيَّانِي فَتَخْزُونِي
(For God's sake [i.e. by God], your cousin — you do not surpass me in lineage, nor are you my master that you should govern me.)
And one asks about the repetition in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيـمِ﴾.
It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: ﴿الرَّحْمٰنُ الرَّحِيـمُ﴾ are two gentle names, one of them gentler than the other: al-Raḥmān is the Gentle, and al-Raḥīm is the One who is kind to His creation with provision.
Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī said: "الرَّحمنُ" towards His creation, "الرحيم" towards His servants in the honour and proof with which He initiated them.
ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī said: He was al-Raḥmān; then when al-Raḥmān was appropriated from among His names, it became "al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm". [Translator's note: the source writes «الخرساني» and «اختزل»; the sense appears to be that the name al-Raḥmān was usurped (by Musaylima, as reported elsewhere), so al-Raḥīm was added; translated as written.]
Al-ʿArzamī said: "الرحمن" towards all creation, "الرحيم" towards the believers.
Abū ʿUbayda said: Both are from al-raḥma (mercy), like their saying nadmān and nadīm (boon companion).
Quṭrub said: It is possible that the two were joined together for tawkīd (emphasis). This is a good view; in emphasis there is the greatest benefit, and it is abundant in the speech of the Arabs, needing no supporting citation.
The benefit in that is what Muḥammad ibn Yazīd said: that it is favour after favour, and bounty after bounty, a strengthening of the hopes of those who call upon Him, and a promise whose hoper is not disappointed.
The view of al-ʿArzamī is also good, because the pattern "fa'lān" contains the meaning of intensiveness (mubālagha); so it is as if — and Allah knows best — He is al-Raḥmān towards all His creation, and for this reason it is applied only to Allah the Exalted, because its meaning is: the One whose mercy encompasses everything.
And for this reason it was placed before "الرحيم".
And "الرحيم" became preferable to al-rāḥim (the one showing mercy), because "الرحيم" is more binding in praise, since it indicates that mercy is permanent in Him, never departing, whereas al-rāḥim applies to one who has shown mercy a single time.
Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā said: "الرحيم" is Arabic and "الرَّحْمَن" is Hebrew, and for this reason the two were joined.
This view is to be turned away from.
Maṭar related from Qatāda concerning His saying ﴿بِسْمِ ٱللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيـمِ﴾ that he said: He praised Himself. And this is a good view.
Abū al-ʿAbbās said: The naʿt (adjective) may occur for praise, as when you say: "Jarīr the poet said."

nahhas-meani:2-2.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ٱلْحَمْدُ للَّهِ﴾. The difference between al-ḥamd (praise) and al-shukr (thanks) is that al-ḥamd is more general, because it applies to commendation (thanāʾ), to glorification (taḥmīd), and to thanks and requital.
Al-shukr is restricted to what is a recompense to one who has done you a kindness; so al-ḥamd is more firmly established in the verse, because it goes beyond thanks.
And it is said: al-ḥamd is a khabar (statement/predication), and the way of a statement is to convey information; so what is the benefit in this?
The answer to this is that Sībawayh said: When a man says "الحمدُ للهِ" with the nominative, it carries the same meaning as his saying "حمدتُ اللهَ حمداً" (I have praised Allah with praise), except that the one who puts al-ḥamd in the nominative states that praise — from him and from all creation — belongs to Allah the Exalted, while the one who puts al-ḥamd in the accusative states that praise from him alone is to Allah the Exalted.
Ibn Kaysān said: This is very good speech, because your saying "الحمدُ للهِ" has the same grammatical form as your saying "المالُ لزيدٍ" (the wealth belongs to Zayd), and its meaning is that you have stated it while intending to be one who praises, not one who reports something; so in the speaker's stating this there is an acknowledgment from him that Allah the Exalted is entitled to it from His creation; thus he is the most praising of those who praise Him, since he acknowledges that praise belongs to Him. So the meaning of the nominative comes back to the same as the meaning of the accusative, and exceeds it in that he has made the praise that comes from his own act and the act of others belong to Allah the Exalted.
Someone other than Sībawayh said: This is spoken only as a seeking of the pardon and forgiveness of Allah the Exalted, and as an extolling and glorifying of Him; so it is contrary to the meaning of a statement, and contains the meaning of a request.
And in the ḥadīth: "Whoever is occupied with remembering Me from asking of Me, I shall give him the best of what I give those who ask."
And it was said: His praising of Himself, Majestic and Mighty, and His commending of Himself, is so that His servants may know that; so the meaning on this view is: Say: praise belongs to Allah.
The self-praise of a human being is only faulted because he is deficient: if he says "I am generous", there is stinginess there; and if he says "I am brave", there is cowardice there; and Allah the Exalted is free of that. For the human being praises himself only to gain a benefit or ward off harm, and Allah the Exalted has no need of this.
* And His saying, Majestic and Mighty: ﴿رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾.
The lexicographers said: al-rabb is the owner (al-mālik), and they cited:
وَهُوَ الرَبُّ والشَّهِيدُ عَلَى يَوْ * مِ الحِيَارَيْنِ وَالبَلاءُ بَلاَءُ
(And he is the lord and the witness over the day of al-Ḥiyārayn, and the trial was a [true] trial.)
The origin of this is that one says rabbahu, yarubbuhu, rabban, and he is rābb and rabb, when he undertakes its proper upkeep.
And one says, for intensiveness: rabbāhu, rabbabahu and rabbatahu.
ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning ﴿رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ that he said: the jinn and humankind.
Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas related from Abū al-ʿĀliya, who said: The jinn are a world (ʿālam), and humankind are a world, and besides that, the earth has four corners, in each corner one thousand five hundred worlds whom Allah created for His worship.
Abū ʿUbayda said: ﴿ربُّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾, i.e. of the created beings.
And al-ʿAjjāj recited: "فخندفٌ هامةُ هذا العالم" (So Khindif are the head of this world).
The first view is the most eminent of these views and the best known in the language, because this plural is the plural of rational beings specifically.
And "عالم" is derived from al-ʿalāma (sign).
Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿalam, al-ʿalāma and al-maʿlam are what indicate a thing; so the world (al-ʿālam) indicates that it has a Creator and Disposer.

nahhas-meani:4-4.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿مَلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ﴾, and it is also read ﴿مَـٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ﴾.
Abū Ḥātim chose (مَالكِ). He said: It is more comprehensive than (مَلِكِ), because you say: Allah is mālik (owner) of the people, mālik of the birds, mālik of the wind, and mālik of every single thing and every kind of thing; whereas one does not say: Allah is malik (king) of the birds, nor malik of the wind, and the like; "مَلِك" is only fitting with "the people" alone.
The eminent lexicographers disagreed with him in that, among them "Abū ʿUbayd" and Abū al-ʿAbbās "Muḥammad ibn Yazīd", and they argued from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿لِّمَنِ ٱلْمُلْكُ ٱلْيَوْمَ﴾? Al-mulk is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of al-malik, while the maṣdar of al-mālik is "milk" with a kasra; and this is a good argument.
Moreover, the argument of "Abū Ḥātim" is not binding, because "malik of the birds" and "of the winds" is not used only because there is no meaning of praise in it.
Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad narrated to us from Abū Dāwūd ibn al-Anbārī, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us from Asbāṭ from al-Suddī — he is Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Mālik [Translator's note: al-Suddī is usually named Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Karīma; translated as written] — from Abū Mālik, and from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, and from Murra al-Hamdānī from Ibn Masʿūd, and from people among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: ﴿مَـٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ﴾: "the Day of al-Dīn" is the Day of Reckoning.
Mujāhid said: ﴿الدِّينُ﴾ is the requital (al-jazāʾ); and the two meanings are one, because the Day of Resurrection is the Day of Reckoning and the Day of Requital.
Al-dīn in other than this is obedience, and al-dīn is custom, as he said:
* أَهَذَا دِينُهُ أَبَداً ودِينِي"؟ *
(Is this ever to be his custom and mine?)
The meanings are close to one another, because when one obeys, one has submitted (dāna).
Custom runs the course of al-dīn; and "so-and-so is in the dīn of so-and-so" means: in his authority and obedience.
If it is said: Why was the Resurrection singled out for this?
The answer is: The Day of Resurrection is a day on which creatures are compelled to know that the whole matter belongs to Allah the Exalted.
And it was said: He singled it out because in this world there are kings and tyrants, while on the Day of Resurrection the whole matter returns to Allah the Exalted alone.

nahhas-meani:5-5.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ﴾ — and He did not say "نَعْبُدكَ", because this is more emphatic.
Sībawayh said: It is as if they put first that whose clarification matters more to them and with whose clarification they are more concerned, even if both matter to them and concern them.
Worship (al-ʿibāda) in the language is obedience with abasement and submission. One says ṭarīq muʿabbad (a beaten road) when it has been made smooth by treading, and baʿīr muʿabbad (a tarred camel) when it has been smeared with tar, i.e. it has been put to menial use as a slave (ʿabd) is put to menial use. Ṭarafa said:
إلَى أَنْ تَحَامَتْنِي العَشِيرَةُ كُلُّهَا * وَأُفْرِدْتُ إفْرَادَ البَعِيرِ المعَبَّدِ
(Until the whole clan shunned me and I was set apart as the tarred camel is set apart.)
And one says ʿabida min kadhā, i.e. he disdained it, as the poet said:
* "وَأَعْبَدُ أَنْ تُهْجَى تَمِيمٌ بِدَارِمِ" *
(And I disdain that Tamīm be satirised by means of Dārim.)
* Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وإيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾.
He repeated "إيَّاكَ" for tawkīd (emphasis), and did not say "ونستعين", just as one says "the wealth is between Zayd and between ʿAmr", repeating "between" for emphasis. And He said ﴿إيَّاكَ﴾ and did not say "إيَّاه" (Him), because the meaning is: Say, O Muḥammad: "إيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ".
Besides, the Arabs turn from the third person to direct address, as al-Aʿshā said:
عِنْدَهُ الحَزْمُ والتُّقَى وَأَسَى الصَرْ * عِ وَحَمْلٌ لمضْلِعِ الأَثْقَالِ
(With him are resolve, piety, consolation for the fallen, and the bearing of crushing burdens.)
Then he said, turning from the third person to address:
ووفاءٌ اذَا أَجَرْتَ فَما غُرَّ * تْ حبالٌ وصَلْتَها بحبالِ
(And faithfulness: when you grant protection, no ropes you have tied to [other] ropes are betrayed.)
And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَسَقَاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَرَاباً طَهُوراً﴾.
Then He said: ﴿إنَّ هَذَا كَانَ لَكُمْ جَزَاءً﴾.
And the reverse of this: the Arabs turn from address to the third person, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿حَتَّىٰ إِذَا كُنتُمْ فِي ٱلْفُلْكِ وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِم بِرِيحٍ طَيِّبَةٍ﴾.
In the speech there is an omission, and the meaning is: and You alone we ask for help in that.

nahhas-meani:6-6.t:
He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَاطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾.
And they are already upon guidance, i.e. [the meaning is] make us firm, as you say to someone standing: "Stand until I come back to you", i.e. remain standing.
The meaning of ﴿ٱهْدِنَا﴾ is: guide us aright (arshidnā). The origin of hadā is arshada (to guide aright), and from it is: ﴿وَٱهْدِنَآ إِلَىٰ سَوَآءِ ٱلصِّرَاطِ﴾. Hadā may mean bayyana (to make clear), as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَأَمَّا ثَمُودُ فَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ﴾; and hadā may mean alhama (to inspire), as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿ٱلَّذِيۤ أَعْطَىٰ كُلَّ شَيءٍ خَلْقَهُ ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ﴾, i.e. He inspired it with what is good for it.
And it was said: [it means] approaching the female.
And hadā may mean daʿā (to call), as He said: ﴿وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هَادٍ﴾, i.e. a prophet who calls them.
The origin of all this is arshada; and the meaning is: guide us aright to the straight path.
Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar al-Anbārī narrated to us, saying: Hāshim ibn al-Qāsim al-Ḥarrānī narrated to me, saying: Abū Isḥāq al-Naḥwī narrated to us from Ḥamza ibn Ḥabīb from Ḥumrān ibn Aʿyan from Abū Manṣūr, the nephew of al-Ḥārith, from al-Ḥārith from ʿAlī, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The straight path is the Book of Allah."
Misʿar related from Manṣūr from Abū Wāʾil from ʿAbd Allāh concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَاطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ that he said: The Book of Allah.
ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAqīl related from Jābir, who said: It is Islam.
Al-ṣirāṭ in the language is the clear road; and the Book of Allah is like the clear road, and likewise Islam. Jarīr said:
أَمِيرُ المُؤمِنِينَ عَلَى صِرَاطٍ * إذا اعْوَجَّ المَوَارِدُ، مُسْتَقِيمِ
(The Commander of the Faithful is on a path that is straight when the watering-tracks go crooked.)
أَمِيرَ المُؤمِنِينَ جَمَعْتَ دِيناً * وَحِلْماً فَاضِلاً لِذَوِي الحُلُومِ
(O Commander of the Faithful, you have combined religion and a forbearance surpassing that of the forbearing.)

safi-cedvel:1-1.t:
* I'rab:
(بسم) a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted khabar (predicate). The mubtadaʾ (subject) is omitted, its implied form being "ابتدائي" (my beginning).
(الله) the Name of Majesty, muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), genitive (majrūr), and the sign of the genitive is the kasra. (الرحمن) naʿt (adjective) of the Name of Majesty, following it in the genitive. (الرحيم) a second naʿt of the Name of Majesty, following it in the genitive.

* Morphology:
(اسم) contains ibdāl (substitution); its origin is سمو. The weak letter, which is the lām (third radical) of the word, was deleted, and the hamzat al-waṣl (connecting hamza) was substituted for it. The proof of the wāw is its plurals أسماء and أسامي and its diminutive سمىّ. The originals were أسماو, أسامو and سموي, and iʿlāl (weak-letter change) by qalb (conversion) took place in them.
(الله) .. its origin is الإلاه: the vowel of the hamza was transferred to the lām of the definite article, then it was made vowelless; the first alif was deleted because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and the lām was assimilated into the second lām..
The alif after the second lām was deleted because of frequent use. الإله is a maṣdar (verbal noun) from أله يأله, meaning "to worship", and the maṣdar stands in the place of the object, i.e. "the one worshipped".
(الرحمن) a derived adjective of the intensive forms; its pattern is فعلان, from the verb رحم يرحم, of the class of فرح.
(الرحيم) a derived adjective of the intensive forms, or an adjective resembling the active participle (ṣifa mushabbaha); its pattern is فعيل, from the verb رحم يرحم.

* Rhetoric:
1- Repetition (al-takrīr): Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, repeated the mention of الرحمن الرحيم because mercy is the bestowal of favour on one in need. He had mentioned the Bestower without those on whom favour is bestowed, so He repeated it together with mentioning them and said: «ربّ العالمين الرحمن» to them all.
2- He, Glorified is He, put الرحمن before الرحيم although الرحمن is more intensive than الرحيم, while it is the custom of the Arabs in attributes of praise to ascend from the lower to the higher, as in their saying: "So-and-so is a learned man, a consummate scholar (عالم نحرير)". That is because it is a name exclusive to Allah the Exalted, like the word «الله», and because when He said «الرحمن» it covered the great and mighty favours and their roots, and He followed it with «الرحيم» as a completion and a sequel, to cover the fine and subtle among them. What belongs to the great and mighty favours and their roots is more deserving of being put first than what indicates their fine points and branches. And singling out these two noble attributes for mention is to set the chain of mercy in motion.
By the name of Allah the Exalted the meanings of things are completed, and from the lamp-niche of بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ the lights of splendour shine upon the pages of the universes.

* Benefits:
The Basmala:
The scholars took care to study the Basmala from all its aspects, of which we mention in particular:
1- They differed over whether it is a verse of the Book of Allah or not. Ibn Masʿūd, Mālik, the Ḥanafīs and the readers of Medina, Basra and Syria do not consider it a verse.
Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, al-Shāfiʿī and the readers of Mecca and Kufa consider it a verse of every sūra.
2- The Basmala was revealed in parts: the first part in the saying of the Exalted: «بِسْمِ اللَّهِ مَجْراها وَمُرْساها»; the second in His saying: «ادْعُوا اللَّهَ أَوِ ادْعُوا الرَّحْمنَ»; the third in His saying: «إِنَّهُ مِنْ سُلَيْمانَ وَإِنَّهُ بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ».

safi-cedvel:2-2.t:
* I'rab:
(الحمد) mubtadaʾ (subject), nominative (marfūʿ). (لله) a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to (mutaʿalliq) an omitted khabar (predicate) of the mubtadaʾ, its implied form being ثابت (established) or واجب (due). (ربّ) naʿt (adjective) [Note: or badal (substitute) of the Name of Majesty.] of the Name of Majesty, following it in the genitive, and the sign of the genitive is the kasra. (العالمين) muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), genitive (majrūr), and the sign of the genitive is the yāʾ, because it is assimilated to the sound masculine plural.
The clause «الحمد لله..» has no grammatical position, being initial (ibtidāʾiyya).

* Morphology:
(الحمد) a heard (samāʿī) maṣdar (verbal noun) of the verb حمد يحمد, of the class of نصر; its pattern is فعل, with fatḥa then sukūn. (ربّ) a maṣdar of يرب, of the class of نصر, then used as an adjective, like عدل and خصم; its pattern is فعل, with fatḥa then sukūn.
(العالمين) plural of العالم, which is a collective noun (ism jamʿ) having no singular from its own letters. It is derived either from العلم (with kasra on the ʿayn) or from العلامة; its pattern is فاعل with fatḥa on the ʿayn, and likewise its plural.

* Rhetoric:
1- The clause الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ is a statement (khabar), but it is used to perform (inshāʾ) the praise, and the benefit of the nominal clause is the perpetuity, continuity and constancy of the praise. In His saying «لله» there is the device of specification (al-ikhtiṣāṣ), to indicate that all praises are exclusive to Him, Glorified and Exalted is He.
2- Since He, Glorified and Exalted is He, opened His Book with the Basmala, which is a kind of praise, it was fitting that He follow it with the comprehensive, universal praise encompassing all its individual instances and reaching the utmost degree of perfection.
3- As for Allah the Exalted praising Himself, it is a statement that He deserves praise and a command to it, or it is said on the tongues of the servants, or it is a figurative expression for the manifestation of the attributes of perfection, which is the ultimate goal of praise.
Praise has been put before the Majestic Name because the context calls for a singular concern with it, even though the mention of Allah the Exalted is more important in itself, and importance calls for putting first.

* Benefits:
Al-Fātiḥa:
Its benefits can hardly be counted; we choose from them:
1- The revelation brought it down twice: the first in Mecca when the prayer was made obligatory.
The second in Medina when the qibla was changed.
2- Al-Fātiḥa has several names: Fātiḥat al-Kitāb (the Opening of the Book), Umm al-Qurʾān (the Mother of the Qur'an), Umm al-Kitāb (the Mother of the Book), Sūrat al-Kanz (the Sūra of the Treasure), Sūrat al-Ḥamd (Praise), al-Shukr (Thanks) and al-Duʿāʾ (Supplication), Sūrat al-Ṣalāh (the Prayer), Sūrat al-Shifāʾ (Healing), and al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī (the Seven Oft-Repeated).
3- The style of iltifāt (shift of address) occurs in this sūra: it began by speaking of the absent, then turned to the style of direct address, and this is one of the kinds of eloquence common in the speech of the Arabs.
4- Al-Fātiḥa contains the basic universals of the Islamic conception, and for that reason Allah made its repetition obligatory in every prayer, indeed in every rakʿa.
It has come in the hadith of Muslim from Abū Hurayra from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ his saying: «Allah the Exalted says: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves: half of it is for Me and half of it is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked. When the servant says: الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ, Allah says: My servant has praised Me. And when he says: الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ, Allah says: My servant has extolled Me.
When he says: مالِكِ يَوْمِ, Allah says: My servant has glorified Me. And when he says: اهْدِنَا الصِّراطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ صِراطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ, He says: This is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asked».

safi-cedvel:3-3.t:
* I'rab:
(الرحمن) naʿt (adjective) of the Name of Majesty [Note: or badal (substitute) of the Name of Majesty, and likewise الرحيم.]. (الرحيم) a second naʿt of the Name of Majesty.

safi-cedvel:4-4.t:
* I'rab:
(مالك) naʿt (adjective) of the Name of Majesty [Note: or badal (substitute) of the Name of Majesty.], genitive (majrūr) like it. (يوم) muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), genitive, and the sign of the genitive is the kasra.
(الدين) muḍāf ilayhi, genitive, and the sign of the genitive is the kasra.

* Morphology:
(مالك) active participle of ملك يملك, in the sense of the ṣifa mushabbaha (adjective resembling the participle) because of the permanence of the ownership; of the class of ضرب; its pattern is فاعل; its plurals are ملّاك and مالكون.
(يوم) a noun meaning the defined time from sunrise to sunset, or an undefined time. Here it comes in the sense of the Day of Resurrection. Its plural is أيّام, and the plural of the plural is أياويم.
(الدين) maṣdar (verbal noun) of دان يدين, of the class of ضرب, meaning "to requite" and "to obey" or "to submit"; its pattern is فعل, with kasra on the fāʾ and sukūn on the ʿayn. There is another maṣdar of the verb, namely ديانة with kasra on the dāl. الدين means requital or obedience, and it may mean religion (al-milla) or custom.

safi-cedvel:5-5.t:
* I'rab:
(إيّاك) an overt, detached pronoun, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa, in the position of the accusative as a fronted mafʿūl bihi (direct object); or (إيّا) is an indeclinable pronoun in the position of the accusative as mafʿūl bihi, and (الكاف) is a particle of address. (نعبد) imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ), and the fāʿil (agent) is a latent (mustatir) pronoun, obligatorily so, its implied form being نحن (we). (الواو) is a conjunction. (إياك نستعين) is parsed like the preceding.
The clause «إياك نعبد..» has no grammatical position, being resumptive (istiʾnāfiyya).
The clause «إياك نستعين..» has no grammatical position, being conjoined (maʿṭūfa) to the clause إياك نعبد.

* Morphology:
(نستعين) contains iʿlāl (weak-letter change); its origin is نستعون, from العون, with kasra on the wāw. The kasra was felt heavy on the wāw, so it was transferred to the ʿayn and the wāw was made vowelless — this is iʿlāl by taskīn (making vowelless) — then the wāw was converted to yāʾ because it is vowelless and preceded by a kasra — this is iʿlāl by qalb (conversion).

* Rhetoric:
1- Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, repeated «إيّاك» because, had He omitted it in the second, the benefit of the fronting would have been lost, namely cutting off the sharing between the two governing verbs. For had He said: «إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ ونستعين», it would not have been clear whether the implied meaning is "إيّاك نعبد وإيّاك نستعين" or "إيّاك نعبد ونستعينك". And He did not say نستعينك, although it would serve to cut off the sharing between the two governing verbs, so that it would convey restriction (al-ḥaṣr) between the two governing verbs.
He put worship before seeking help, although seeking help comes first — because the servant seeks the help of Allah in worship so that He may help him in it — because the wāw does not require order, and seeking help is the fruit of worship, and because presenting the means before asking for the need is so that they may merit having it answered.
2- The iltifāt (shift) in this noble verse is a shift from the absent (third person) to the second person, a variation of the composition from one mode to another, running according to the way of eloquence in diversifying speech and the path of excellence as the context requires. For moving from one style to another is more effective in drawing souls and winning hearts; it occurs from each of the first person, the second person and the third person to each of the other two, as in the saying of the Exalted «اللَّهُ الَّذِي أَرْسَلَ الرِّياحَ فَتُثِيرُ سَحاباً».
3- Preferring the form of the speaker together with others in the two verbs is to announce the speaker's own shortcoming and his unfitness to stand alone in the stations of grandeur, presenting worship and calling for help and guidance independently; and that this is conceivable only from a band of which he is one and a group of whose company he is part, as is the custom of kings. Or it is to indicate that all the monotheists share with him in the state that has come upon him, based on the mutual support of the proofs compelling that.

safi-cedvel:6-6.t:
* I'rab:
(اهد) imperative verb of supplication, indeclinable (mabnī) on the deletion of the weak letter, and (نا) is an attached pronoun, indeclinable, in the position of the accusative as mafʿūl bihi (direct object); the fāʿil (agent) is a latent (mustatir) pronoun, obligatorily so, its implied form being أنت (you). (الصراط) second mafʿūl bihi, accusative (manṣūb), and the sign of the accusative is the fatḥa [Note: The verb (هدى) is transitive to the second object without a preposition, or with the preposition اللام, or with the preposition إلى. It is stated in al-Muḥīṭ: هداه الله الطريق, وله, وإليه.].
(المستقيم) naʿt (adjective) of الصراط, accusative like it, and the sign of the accusative is the fatḥa.
The clause has no grammatical position, being resumptive (istiʾnāfiyya).

* Morphology:
(اهدنا) contains iʿlāl (weak-letter change) by deletion, to suit the indeclinability; its origin in the nominative imperfect is تهدينا. The pattern of اهدنا is افعنا. (الصراط) is with sīn and with ṣād; in the reading with ṣād there is ibdāl (substitution), as the sīn was converted to ṣād to harmonise with the ṭāʾ in iṭbāq (velarisation).
(المستقيم) active participle of استقام; it is on the pattern of its imperfect, replacing the imperfect prefix with a mīm carrying ḍamma and putting kasra on the letter before the last.. It contains iʿlāl; its origin is مستقوم — with kasra on the wāw — because its bare verb is قام يقوم; then the same happened in it as happened in نستعين.

* Rhetoric:
1- «اهْدِنَا الصِّراطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ»: المستقيم means the level (straight), and what is meant by it is the path of truth, namely the tolerant ḥanīf religion, midway between excess and negligence. The true religion is likened to the straight path, and the point of similarity between them is that Allah, Glorified is He, though exalted above places, yet the servant seeking to arrive must cross distances, so that the arrival and the meeting may be honoured. This is of the type of explicit metaphor (al-istiʿāra al-taṣrīḥiyya).
2- He, Glorified and Exalted is He, repeated the mention of «الصراط» because it is the place prepared for travelling. In the first He mentioned the place without the traveller, so He repeated it with mention of him in His saying «صِراطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ», in which it is made explicit what excludes the Jews, who are those who incurred wrath, and the Christians, who are those astray.

safi-cedvel:7-7.t:
* I'rab:
(صراط) badal (substitute) of the first صراط, following it in the accusative, and the sign of its accusative is the fatḥa. (الذين) relative noun, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa, in the position of the genitive as muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct). (أنعمت) past verb, indeclinable on the sukūn because it is attached to a nominative pronoun, and (التاء) is an attached pronoun in the position of the nominative as fāʿil (agent). (عليهم): (على) is a preposition and (الهاء) is an attached pronoun, indeclinable on the kasra, in the position of the genitive by (على), attached to (mutaʿalliq) (أنعمت); and (الميم) is a particle for the masculine plural. (غير) badal of the relative noun (الذين), following it in the genitive [Note: Or badal of the pronoun in (عليهم), or naʿt (adjective) of the relative noun. This last is rejected by al-Mubarrad, because (غير) for him can only be indefinite even if it is put in construct, the construct in it being merely verbal (lafẓiyya), while (الذين) is definite.. This objection has been answered with two answers:
The first: that (غير) is indefinite when it does not fall between two opposites; but when it does — as in the preceding verse — the otherness is confined, and so it becomes definite through the construct.
The second: that the relative noun resembles indefinite nouns in the vagueness it contains, so it was treated as indefinite nouns are treated.]. (المغضوب) muḍāf ilayhi, genitive. (عليهم) like the first, in the position of the nominative as nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) of المغضوب. (الواو) a conjunction. (لا) redundant (zāʾida), to emphasise the negation. (الضالّين) maʿṭūf (conjoined) to (غير), genitive like it, and the sign of the genitive is the yāʾ because it is a sound masculine plural.
The clause أنعمت عليهم ... has no grammatical position, being the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative noun.

* Morphology:
(المغضوب) passive participle of غضب, of the class of فرح; its pattern is مفعول.
(الضالّين) plural of الضال, which is the active participle of ضلّ يضلّ, of the class of ضرب; its pattern is فاعل, and the ʿayn of the word was assimilated into its lām because they are the same letter.
(غير) a noun that is always singular and masculine; it may be a naʿt (adjective) and it may be a particle of exception..
If a feminine is intended by it, it is permissible to make the verb attributed to it feminine. You say: قامت غير هند, meaning thereby a woman.. It is always in construct, overtly and implicitly. So putting the alif and lām on it is an error.

* Rhetoric:
1- Explanation after vagueness (al-tafsīr baʿd al-ibhām): in this noble verse, where it is made clear that the straight path — its exposition and explanation — is the path of the Muslims, so that this is a testimony to the path of the Muslims as being straight in the most eloquent manner; as you say: "Shall I direct you to the most generous and most excellent of people? So-and-so." This is more eloquent in describing him with generosity and excellence than your saying:
"Shall I direct you to So-and-so, the most generous, the most excellent?" because you have mentioned him twice, first in summary and second in detail, and you made So-and-so an explanation and clarification of "the most generous, the most excellent", and so you made him a byword for generosity and excellence.
2- Rhyming (al-tasjīʿ): in الرحيم and المستقيم, and in نستعين and الضالين. Tasjīʿ is the agreement of two words in pattern and in the rhyme letter (al-rawī).
3- And if we consider what is the benefit of the entry of «لا» in the saying of the Exalted «وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ», although the speech without it would suffice for the purpose: it is to emphasise the negation conveyed by «غير».
4- The opening (al-istihlāl):
Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, opened the Qur'an with al-Fātiḥa, and istihlāl is one of the finest and most elegant devices of rhetoric. Its definition: that the speaker begins his speech with what points to the intended aim without being explicit, but by a subtle allusion.
5- Turning away from attributing anger to Him the Exalted, as was done with bestowing favour, follows the method of the courtesies of the revelation in attributing favours and good things to Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, but not their opposites, as in the saying of the Exalted: الَّذِي خَلَقَنِي فَهُوَ يَهْدِينِ وَالَّذِي هُوَ يُطْعِمُنِي وَيَسْقِينِ وَإِذا مَرِضْتُ فَهُوَ يَشْفِينِ

semin-durr:3-3.t: [Translator's note: the source entry begins here without restating the Quranic words; it concerns {الرحمن الرحيم} in this ayah.] A naʿt (adjective) or a badal (substitute). They have also been read in the accusative and in the nominative, and the justification of that is what was mentioned under {رَبِّ العالمين}. The discussion of their derivation has already come under the Basmala, which makes it unnecessary to repeat it.

semin-durr:6-6.t:
The words of Allah the Exalted: {اهدنا الصراط} to the end of it: اهْدِ is an imperative form whose meaning is supplication (duʿāʾ). This form occurs with many meanings which the legal theorists (al-uṣūliyyūn) have mentioned. One of them said: if the form افعَلْ comes from a superior to an inferior it is called a command (amr); in the reverse case, a supplication (duʿāʾ); and from an equal, a request (iltimās). Its fāʿil (agent) is obligatorily latent (mustatir), for the reason given earlier, i.e. "guide, You". And نا is the first mafʿūl bihi (direct object); it is an attached pronoun used for the speaker together with others, or for one who speaks of himself in the plural of majesty. It is used in the position of the nominative, the accusative and the genitive with a single form, as in: قُمنَا, ضرَبَنَا زيدٌ and مَرَّ بنا, and no other pronoun shares this peculiarity with it. Some people have claimed that the yāʾ is likewise; you say: أكرمَنَي, مرِّ بي and أنت تقومين يا هند; the yāʾ in the first example is in the position of the accusative, in the second in the position of the genitive, and in the third in the position of the nominative. This is worthless, because the yāʾ in the nominative is not the same yāʾ as the one in the accusative and the genitive: the latter is for the speaker, while this one is for the feminine addressee. It has also been said: rather, the word «هُمْ» shares it; you say: هم نائمون, ضربَهم and مررت بهم, so «هم» is in the position of the nominative, the accusative and the genitive with a single form, and it is for the absent (third person plural) in every case. Although this is closer than the first, in the nominative it is a detached pronoun, while in the accusative and genitive it is an attached pronoun, so the two differ — unlike «نا», whose meaning does not differ and which is an attached pronoun in all three cases. [Translator's note: the source prints «ن» for the pronoun نا in two places; rendered here as نا.]
والصراطَ is the second mafʿūl bihi, and المستقيمَ is its naʿt (adjective); it has followed it in four of the ten things mentioned [Translator's note: i.e. the ten features of agreement between an adjective and its noun — case, definiteness, gender, number, etc.].
The basic usage of «هَدَى» is that it is transitive to the first object by itself and to the second by a preposition, which is either إلى or the lām, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: {وَإِنَّكَ لتهدي إلى صِرَاطٍ مُّسْتَقِيمٍ} [al-Shūrā: 52] and {يِهْدِي لِلَّتِي هِيَ أَقْوَمُ} [al-Isrāʾ: 9]. Then latitude is taken with it, the preposition is dropped, and it becomes transitive by itself. So the underlying form of اهدنا الصراط is اهدنا للصراط or إلى الصراطِ, and then [the preposition] was dropped. [Translator's note: the source repeats the word الحرفُ by a printing error.]
The imperative, according to the Basrans, is indeclinable (mabnī), and according to the Kufans it is declinable (muʿrab). They claim that in a word like «اضرب» the underlying form is لِتَضْرِب, with the lām of command; then the jussive-governing particle was dropped, followed by the imperfect prefix, and the connecting hamza (hamzat al-waṣl) was brought in because one cannot begin with a vowelless letter. This is something there is no need for, and refuting them has a more fitting place.
The pattern of اهْدِ is افْعِ: its final radical, the yāʾ, has been dropped, treating the imperative like the jussive (majzūm), and in the jussive the final radical is dropped when it is a weak letter.
Al-hidāya (guidance) is directing (irshād), or indicating (dalāla), or going ahead (taqaddum); from this come هَوادِي الخيل ("the leaders of the horses"), because they go ahead. Imruʾ al-Qays said:
67 - فَأَلْحَقَه بالهاديات ودونَه ... جواحِرُها في صَرَّةٍ لم تَزَيًّلِ
(He brought him up with the leading ones [of the herd], while the laggards were left behind him in a close pack that did not scatter.)
Or making clear (tabyīn), as in: {وَأَمَّا ثَمُودُ فَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ} [Fuṣṣilat: 17], i.e. We made clear to them; or inspiration (ilhām), as in: {أعطى كُلَّ شَيءٍ خَلْقَهُ ثُمَّ هدى} [Ṭā Hā: 50], i.e. He inspired it toward what is good for it; or calling (duʿāʾ), as in the words of Allah the Exalted: {وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هَادٍ} [al-Raʿd: 7], i.e. a caller. It has also been said that it is inclining (mayl), and from it is {إِنَّا هُدْنَآ إِلَيْكَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 56], the meaning being: incline our hearts to You. This is a mistake, for that is a different root, from هادَ يَهُود. [Translator's note: the reference as printed is al-Aʿrāf: 56; the verse is al-Aʿrāf 7:156.] Al-Rāghib said: "Hidāya is guidance with gentleness; from it come al-hadiyya (the gift) and هوادي الوحش, i.e. the foremost wild animals that lead others. Guidance in the sense of indicating is specified with هَدَيتُ, and that in the sense of giving with أَهْديت."
Al-ṣirāṭ is the easy-to-travel road; some do not restrict it to being easy to travel. [The poet] said:
68 - فَضَلَّ عن نَهْج الصراطِ الواضِحِ ...
(So he strayed from the course of the clear road.)
And similarly:
69 - أميرُ المؤمنين على صِراطٍ ... إذا اعْوَجَّ المَوارِدُ مستقيمِ
(The Commander of the Faithful is on a straight road when the watering-paths go crooked.)
Another said:
70 - شَحَنَّا أرضَهم بالخيلِ حتى ... تَرَكْناهُمْ أَذَلَّ من الصِّراطِ
(We filled their land with horses until we left them more trodden-down than the road.)
i.e. the road. It is derived from al-sirṭ, which is swallowing: either because the one travelling it swallows it up, or because it swallows up the one who travels it. Do you not see their saying: "The one who knows a land kills it, and a land kills the one ignorant of it"? On these two considerations Abū Tammām said:
71 - رَعَتْه الفيافي بعدما كان حِقْبةً ... رعاها وماءُ المُزْنِ يَنْهَلُّ ساكِبُهْ
(The deserts grazed upon him after he had for a long time grazed upon them, while the water of the rain-clouds poured down.)
On this basis the road was called لَقَم and مُلْتَقِم, because it gobbles up the one travelling it, or the one travelling it gobbles it up.
Its original letter is the sīn, and Qunbul read it so wherever it occurs. It was changed into ṣād only because of the elevated letter (ḥarf al-istiʿlāʾ) [i.e. the ṭāʾ], and changing it into ṣād is regular in this circumstance, as in صَقَر for سَقَر, صُلْح for سُلْح, إصْبَع for اسبَع and مُصَيْطِر for مُسَيْطر, because of the closeness between the two.
The ṣād in الصراط and the like may be given a tinge of zāy (ishmām), and Khalaf read it so wherever it occurs, and Khallād only in the first occurrence; it may also be read as a pure zāy. In the Muṣḥaf it is written only with ṣād, despite their differing readings of it, as stated above.
Al-ṣirāṭ is treated as masculine and feminine: the masculine is the dialect of Tamīm and the feminine the dialect of the Ḥijāz. If it is used as masculine, its plural of paucity is أَفْعِلة and its plural of multitude فُعُل, as in حِمار, أَحْمِرة and حُمُر; if it is used as feminine, its analogical plural is أَفْعُل, as in ذِراع and أَذْرُع. Al-mustaqīm is the active participle of استقام in the sense of the bare verb; its meaning is "level, without crookedness". Its underlying form is مُسْتَقْوِم, then it underwent the same weak-letter change (iʿlāl) as نَسْتعين. The full discussion of its root will come at the words of Allah the Exalted: {يُقِيمُونَ الصلاة}.

semin-durr:5-5.t:
«إياك» is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) placed before «نَعْبُدُ»; it was put first for restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), and it must be a detached pronoun. They disagreed about it: is it of the category of overt nouns or of pronouns? The majority hold that it is a pronoun, while al-Zajjāj said: "It is an overt noun." The arguments for preferring each of the two views are mentioned in the books of grammar.
Those who say it is a pronoun disagreed about it in four views. The first: that the whole of it is the pronoun. The second: that «إيَّا» alone is the pronoun, and what follows it is a noun in the position of muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct), making clear what is intended by it — first person, third person or second person. The third: that «إيَّا» alone is the pronoun, and what follows it are particles that make clear what is intended by it. The fourth: that «إيَّا» is a support (ʿimād), and what follows it is the pronoun. Its annexation to an overt noun occurs anomalously in their saying: «إذا بلغ الرجلُ الستين فإياه وإيَّا الشَوابِّ» ("When a man reaches sixty, let him beware of young women"), with «إيا» annexed to الشَوابِّ; and this supports the view of whoever makes the kāf, the hāʾ and the yāʾ in the position of the genitive when you say: إياك, إياه, إياي.
Some grammarians went far astray and assigned it a derivation, then said: is it derived from «أَوّ», as in the poet's words:
59 - فَأَوِّ لذِكْراها إذا ما ذَكَرْتُها ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(So: ah! at the memory of her whenever I remember her …)
or from «آية», as in his words:
60 - لم يُبْقِ هذا الدهرُ من آيائِهِ ... . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
(This age has left nothing of its signs …)
And is its pattern إفْعَل, or فَعيل, or فَعُول, which morphological change then turned into the form إيَّا? What this speaker mentioned brings no benefit; besides, morphology and derivation do not enter into what is deeply rooted in indeclinability.
There are several dialectal forms of it: the best known is with kasra on the hamza and a doubled yāʾ; among them also is fatḥa on the hamza, and changing it into hāʾ, with the yāʾ doubled or undoubled. The poet said:
61 - فَهِيَّاك والأمرَ الذي إنْ توسَّعَتْ ... مَواردُه ضاقَتْ عليك مصادِرُهْ
(So beware of an affair whose entrances, if they widen, will make its exits narrow upon you.)
[And one of them said: إياك with an undoubled yāʾ is to be avoided], because it would become "Your sun we worship", since إياة of the sun is its light, with kasra on the hamza, and it may take fatḥa. It has also been said: it is to the sun what the halo is to the moon. If you drop the tāʾ you lengthen it. [The poet] said:
62 - سَقَتْه إياةُ الشمسِ إلاَّ لِثاتِه ... أُسِفَّ فلم تَكْدِمْ عليه بإثْمِدِ
(The light of the sun watered it [i.e. made it bright], except for its gums, which were dusted with antimony, and it did not bite upon it.)
Some of these forms have been read as anomalous readings (shādhdh). Pronouns have a long chapter and a wide division which this book cannot bear; only what suits it will come in its course.
And نعبُدُ is an imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ) because it is free of any accusative-governing or jussive-governing particle; it has also been said: because it occupies the place of a noun, and this is the view of the Basrans. The meaning of al-muḍāriʿ is "the resembling one", meaning that it resembles the noun in its vowelled and vowelless letters and in the number of its letters — do you not see that ضارب has the same measure as يَضْرب in what I have mentioned to you? — and in that it is general and becomes specific with respect to times, just as the noun is general and becomes specific with respect to persons. Its fāʿil (agent) is obligatorily latent (mustatir), for the reason given under the Istiʿādha.
Al-ʿibāda (worship) is the utmost self-abasement, and none deserves it except the one who has the utmost bounty, and He is the Creator, Exalted is He. So it is more far-reaching than al-ʿubūdiyya, because al-ʿubūdiyya is the display of self-abasement. One says طريق مُعَبَّد, i.e. a road made level by treading. Ṭarafa said:
63 - تباري عِتاقاً ناجِياتٍ وَأَتْبَعَتْ ... وَظِيفاً وظيفاً فوقَ مَوْرٍ مُعَبَّدِ
(She vies with swift, noble she-camels, placing foot after foot upon a well-trodden road.)
From it comes al-ʿabd (the slave), because of his lowliness, and بعيرٌ مُعَبَّد, i.e. a camel made docile [Translator's note: literally "abased"] by being smeared with tar.
It has also been said: al-ʿibāda is devoting oneself exclusively (al-tajarrud). One says عَبَدْت الله only without doubling, and عَبَّدْتُ الرجلَ only with doubling, i.e. I subdued him or took him as a slave.
In the words of Allah the Exalted {إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ} there is iltifāt (a shift of person) from the third person to the second person, for had the speech run according to its basic pattern, it would have been said: الحمد لله, and then: إياه نعبدُ. [Translator's note: the source prints «الحمد الله», evidently a misprint for الحمد لله.] Iltifāt is a kind of eloquence. Among the instances of iltifāt — though it is the reverse of this — are the words of Allah the Exalted: {حتى إِذَا كُنتُمْ فِي الفلك وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِم} [Yūnus: 22], and He did not say: بكم. Imruʾ al-Qays made three shifts of person in his words:
64 - تطاوَلَ ليلُكَ بالإِثمِدِ ... وبات الخَليُّ ولم تَرْقُدِ
وباتَ وباتَتْ له ليلَةٌ ... كليلة ذي العائِرِ الأرْمَدِ
وذلك من نبأٍ جاءني ... وخُبِّرْتُه عن أَبِي الأسودِ
(Your night has grown long at al-Ithmid, while the carefree one slept and you did not sleep; / And he passed the night, and a night passed for him like the night of one with a mote in his inflamed eye; / And that was because of news that came to me, and I was told it about Abū al-Aswad.)
Someone faulted al-Zamakhsharī for making these three shifts, and said: rather they are two shifts. The first is the departure from the second person with which it opens in his words «ليلُك» to the third person in his words «وباتَتْ له ليلةٌ»; the second is the departure from this third person to the first person in his words «من نبأٍ جاءني وخُبِّرْتُه». The answer is that his first words, «تطاول ليلُك», contain a shift of person, because the basic form of the speech would have been to say: تطاول ليلي, since he himself is the one meant. So he shifted from the position of the speaker to that of the addressee, then from the addressee to the third person, then from the third person to the speaker, which is the original.
It has been read as an anomalous reading: «إِيَّاكَ يُعْبَدُ», with the verb passive and in the third person. Its justification, despite its difficulty, is that it contains a borrowing (istiʿāra) and a shift of person. As for the borrowing: the accusative pronoun was borrowed for the nominative pronoun, the underlying form being أنت تُعْبَدُ ("You are worshipped"). This is common, as in their saying عساك, عساه and عساني according to one of the views, and in the words of another:
65 - يابنَ الزُّبير طالما عَصَيْكا ... وطالَمَا عَنِّيْتَنَا إِلَيكا
(O son of al-Zubayr, how long you have disobeyed, and how long you have made us toil toward you!)
The kāf in «عَصَيْكا» stands in for the tāʾ, the underlying form being عَصَيْتَ. As for the shift of person: this reader ought to have read إياك تُعْبَدُ, in the second person, but he shifted from the second person in «إيَّاك» to the third person in «يُعْبَدُ». This, however, is an unusual shift, because it is within a single sentence, unlike the shift mentioned before. An analogue of this shift is his words:
66 - أأنتَ الهلاليُّ الذي كنتَ مرةً ... سَمِعْنا به والأَرْحَبِيُّ المُغَلَّبُ
(Are you the Hilālī whom we once heard of, and the Arḥabī who was overcome?)
He said «به» after saying «أنت» and «كنت».
