Al-Zamakhsharī inclined to this; he said: "So that the fronting conveys restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), because it came as a rebuttal of the unbelievers who used to begin with the names of their gods, saying: 'In the name of al-Lāt, in the name of al-ʿUzzā'." This is very good. He then raised against himself His saying, Exalted is He: {اقرأ باسم رَبِّكَ} [al-Qalam: 1] [Translator's note: the verse is al-ʿAlaq 96:1; the source labels it al-Qalam, a name sometimes given to this sūra.], where this governing word is stated explicitly before what it governs, and he answered that fronting the verb in Sūrat al-ʿAlaq is more fitting, because it is the first sūra revealed, so the command to recite was more important. Others answered that «باسم ربك» is attached not to the «اقرأ» before it but to the «اقرأ» after it, so it conforms to the aforementioned rule.
This is open to question, because on this view the apparent sense is that the second «اقرأ» is a tawkīd (emphasis) of the first, so the governed element of the emphasising word would have separated it from what it emphasises, in addition to the separation by a long stretch of speech.
They also differed: is that verb an imperative or a statement? Al-Farrāʾ held that it is an imperative, its implied form being: «اقرأ أنت باسم الله» ("recite, you, in the name of Allah"). Al-Zajjāj held that it is a statement, its implied form being: «اقرأ أنا» [Translator's note: so in the source; the intended form is presumably «أقرأ أنا», "I recite".] or «أبتَدِئُ» and the like.

«الله» in «بسم الله» is a muḍāf ilayhi (genitive construct). Is what governs the muḍāf ilayhi the muḍāf, an implied preposition, or the meaning of annexation? There are three views, the best of which is the middle one. It is a proper name (ʿalam) of the One truly worshipped; it is applied to no other, and no created being has dared to take it as a name. Likewise «الإِله», before the transfer [of the hamza's vowel] and the assimilation, is applied only to the One truly worshipped. Al-Zamakhsharī said: "It is as if it became a proper name by predominance (bi-l-ghalaba)." As for «إله» without the alif and lām, it is applied to the One truly worshipped and to others; He, Exalted is He, said: {لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَآ آلِهَةٌ إِلاَّ الله لَفَسَدَتَا} [al-Anbiyāʾ: 22], {وَمَن يَدْعُ مَعَ الله إِلَهَا آخَرَ لاَ بُرْهَانَ لَهُ بِهِ} [al-Muʾminūn: 117], {[أَرَأَيْتَ] مَنِ اتخذ إلهه هَوَاهُ} [al-Furqān: 43].
People differed whether it is murtajal (coined, underived) or derived; the correct view is the first, and it is the most definite of definite nouns. It is related that Sībawayh was seen in a dream and was asked: "What did Allah do with you?" He said: "Much good, because I made His name the most definite of definites."
Then those who hold that it is derived differed greatly. Some said: it is derived from «لاهَ يليه», i.e. to be elevated; hence the sun was called «إلاَهة», with kasra and with fatḥa on the hamza, because of its elevation — or, it was said, because they took it as an object of worship. On this basis it was said «لَهْيَ أبوك», meaning «للهِ أبوك», the ʿayn having been moved to the place of the lām; and he lightened it by dropping the alif and lām and dropping the preposition. Some went far and made from this the poet's saying:
24 - ألا ياسَنا بَرْقٍ على قُلَلِ الحِمى ... لَهِنَّكَ من برقٍ عليَّ كريمُ
(O gleam of lightning over the peaks of al-Ḥimā, by Allah, you are a lightning dear to me!)
He said: the root form is «لله إنك كريمٌ عليَّ»; the preposition, the definite article and the alif before the hāʾ of the Name of Majesty were dropped, the hāʾ was made quiescent, treating continuous speech like a pause, so the word became «لَهْ»; then the vowel of the hamza of «إنَّ» was thrown onto the hāʾ, leaving «لَهِنَّك», as you see. This is an ugliness on the part of the one who said it; there are two views on the verse easier than this.
Some said: "It is derived from «لاه يَلُوه لِياهاً», i.e. to be veiled." On these two views the alif is radical, so the root of the word is «لاَهَ»; then the definite article came onto it, giving «اللاه»; then the lām of the article was assimilated into the following lām, since the conditions of assimilation were met, and its lām was given the heavy (velarised) pronunciation (tafkhīm). Its pattern on the two preceding views is either faʿal or faʿil, with fatḥa or kasra on the ʿayn; on every supposition the weak letter was vowelled and preceded by a fatḥa, so it was changed into alif; the root form was «لَيَهاً», «لَيِهاً», «لَوَهاً» or «لَوِهاً».
Some made it derived from «أَلَه». «أَلَه» is a word shared among several meanings: worship, finding repose, bewilderment and resorting in fear. So the meaning of «إله» is that His creation worship Him, find repose in Him, are bewildered about Him and resort to Him in fear. From it is the saying of Ruʾba:
25 - لِلَّهِ دَرُّ الغانِياتِ المُدَّهِ ... سَبَّحْنَ واسْتَرْجَعْنَ مِنْ تألُّهي
(How excellent are the praising fair maidens! They said "subḥān Allah" and "innā li-llāh" at my devotion.)
i.e. at his worship; and from it is {وَيَذَرَكَ وَآلِهَتَكَ} [al-Aʿrāf: 127], i.e. your worship. The Commander of the Faithful alluded to the meaning of bewilderment in his saying: "The embellishment of descriptions falls short before His attributes, and the turns of language go astray there." That is because when the servant reflects on His attributes he is bewildered; hence it is related: "Reflect on the bounties of Allah, and do not reflect on Allah." On this view the hamza is radical and the alif before the hāʾ is extra, so the root of the noble Name of Majesty is «الإِله», as in the poet's saying:
26 - معاذَ الإِله أن تكونَ كظبيةٍ ... ولا دُمْيَةٍ ولا عَقِيْلَةٍ رَبْرَبِ
(God forbid that she should be like a gazelle, or a statue, or the choicest of a herd of wild cows.)
Then the hamza was dropped owing to frequent use, as it was dropped in «ناس», whose root is «أُناس», as in his saying:
27 - إنَّ المَنايا يَطَّلِعْ ... نَ على الأُناس الآمِنينا
(The fates come suddenly upon people who feel secure.)
So the [lām of the] definite article met the lām, was assimilated into it, and was given tafkhīm. Or we say: the hamza of «الإِله» was dropped by transfer (naql), meaning that we transferred its vowel to the lām of the article and dropped it after transferring its vowel, as is known in naql; then the lām of the article was assimilated, as has been mentioned, except that the transfer here is obligatory owing to frequent use.
Some said: it is derived from «وَلِهَ», since every created being is yearning (wālih) towards Him; on this basis one of the sages said: "Allah is beloved of all things," and this is indicated by His saying, Exalted is He: {وَإِن مِّن شَيْءٍ إِلاَّ يُسَبِّحُ بِحَمْدَهِ} [al-Isrāʾ: 44]. Its root form is «وِلاه»; then the wāw was changed into hamza, as it was changed in «إشاح» and «إعاء», whose roots are «وِشاح» and «وِعاء»; so the word became «إلاهاً», and then what was described above was done to it: dropping its hamza and assimilation. This view is attributed to al-Khalīl. On these two [latter] views the pattern of «إلاه» is fiʿāl, in the sense of mafʿūl (passive participle), i.e. worshipped, or one about whom people are bewildered, like «الكِتاب» in the sense of «مكتوب».
Al-Khalīl's view was rejected on two grounds. First: if the hamza were a substitute for wāw, it would be permissible to pronounce the original, yet no one has said it, whereas they say «إشاح» and «وشاح», «إعاء» and «وعاء». Second: if it were so, it would be pluralised as «أَوْلِهة», like «أَوْعِية» and «أَوشِحَة», with the hamza returned to its original; yet «إله» is pluralised only as «آلهة».
Al-Khalīl can get clear of these two objections by [saying] that the substitution became binding in this noun because it is distinguished by rules in which nothing else shares, as you will see; and then the plural came following the binding substitution.

As for the alif and lām, the discussion of them depends on whether it is derived or not. If the first is held, they were originally the definite article; if the second, they are extra. Their dropping from the Name of Majesty is anomalous in their saying «لاهِ أبوك», whose root is «للهِ أبوك», as mentioned. They said: the alif before the hāʾ was dropped in writing so that it would not resemble the writing of «اللات», the name of the idol, because some change this tāʾ into hāʾ in pause and write it with hāʾ following the pause; hence the resemblance would arise.
It was also said: so that it would not resemble the writing of «اللاه», the active participle of «لها يلهو» (to amuse oneself). This holds only in the dialect of those who drop the yāʾ of the definite defective noun in pause, since writing follows it; but for those who retain it in pause and so retain it in writing, there is no confusion. It was also said: dropping the alif is a rare dialectal usage on which the writing was based, and this was made binding owing to its frequent use. The poet said:
28 - أقبلَ سَيْلٌ كان من أمر اللهْ ... يَحْرِدُ حَرْدَ الجَنَّة المُغِلَّهْ
(A flood came on, from the command of Allah, making for the fruitful garden with determined intent.)
The rule for its lām is tafkhīm, out of reverence, unless preceded by a kasra, in which case it is pronounced light (tarqīq) — even though Abū al-Qāsim al-Zamakhsharī stated tafkhīm without qualification, but he means what I have said. Abū al-Baqāʾ reported that some pronounce it light in every case; this amounts to nothing, because the Arabs, generation after generation, are against it, as al-Zamakhsharī mentioned. The scholars of the readings reported a disagreement where it is preceded by a fatḥa with imāla, i.e. close to kasra: some pronounce it light and some heavy, as in the reading of al-Sūsī in one of his two ways: «حتى نَرَى اللهَ جَهْرةً».
Al-Suhaylī and Ibn al-ʿArabī reported a strange view about it: that the alif and lām in it are radical, not extra; they excused the connective nature of the hamza by frequent use, as al-Khalīl says about the hamza of the definite article. Their view was rejected on the ground that the Name of Majesty would then have to take tanwīn, since its pattern would be faʿʿāl, like «لآَّل» and «سَآَّل», and there is nothing in it to prevent tanwīn; this shows that «أل» in it is extra to the essence of the word.
Among the strange things reported about it as well is that it is not Arabic but Arabicised, of Syriac origin, its root being «لاها», which the Arabs Arabicised, saying «الله». They argued for this from the poet's saying:
29 - كحَلْفَةٍ من أبي رياحِ ... يَسْمَعُها لاهُهُ الكُبارُ
(Like an oath from Abū Riyāḥ, which his great god hears.)
So he brought it in the original form before Arabicisation. Abū Zayd al-Balkhī reported this.
[Among the strange things reported about it as well is that its root is the hāʾ which is the pronoun for the absent one.] They said: that is because they affirmed Him as existing in the view of their intellects, so they pointed to Him with the pronoun; then the lām of possession was added to it, since they knew that He is the Creator and Owner of things, so the word became «لَهُ»; then the alif and lām were added for reverence and magnification. This does not resemble the speech of the lexicographers or the grammarians; it resembles only the speech of some Sufis.
Among the strange things reported about it as well is that it is an adjective, not a noun. The one who held this argued that a name makes the thing named known, while Allah, Exalted is He, is not perceived by the senses nor by intuition, so His name does not make Him known — only His attributes make Him known; and because a proper name stands in place of pointing, and that is impossible in His case, Exalted is He. Al-Zamakhsharī rejected this view with words meaning that you describe it but do not describe with it: you say «إله عظيم واحد» ("a great, one God"), as you say «شيءٌ عظيم» and «رجلٌ كريم», but you do not say «شيء إله», just as you do not say «شيء رجل»; were it an adjective, it would occur as an adjective of something else, not as a qualified noun. Further, His beautiful attributes must have a qualified noun to which they apply; if you made all of them adjectives, they would remain not applied to any noun qualified by them. And there is no disagreement about anything other than the Name of Majesty being an adjective; so it is settled that the Name of Majesty is a noun, not an adjective.
The discussion of this noble name admits of more length than I have mentioned to you; I abridged it only for fear of wearying the reader of this book.

«الرحمن الرحيم»: two adjectives derived from «الرحمة» (mercy). It was also said: «الرحمن» is not derived, because the Arabs did not know it, in their saying: {وَمَا الرحمن} [al-Furqān: 60]. Ibn al-ʿArabī answered this by [saying] that they were ignorant of the attribute, not of the One it qualifies; that is why they did not say: «ومَنْ الرحمن» ("and who is al-Raḥmān?"). The two follow the noun they qualify in four of the ten [things] mentioned. [Translator's note: this refers to the ten features (case, definiteness, number, gender, etc.) in four of which a naʿt agrees with its noun, as set out earlier in the author's introduction.]
Al-Aʿlam al-Shantamarī held that «الرحمن» is a badal (substitute) for the name Allah, not a naʿt (adjective) of it; this rests on his view that «الرحمن» is a proper name by predominance. He argued for this from its occurring without following a qualified noun, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {الرحمن عَلَّمَ القرآن} [al-Raḥmān: 1-2], {الرحمن عَلَى العرش استوى} [Ṭā Hā: 5]. Al-Suhaylī rejected this, [saying] that were it a badal it would clarify what precedes it, while what precedes it — the Name of Majesty — needs no clarification, since it is the most definite of proper names; do you not see that they said {وَمَا الرحمن} [al-Furqān: 60] and did not say «وما اللهُ»? End of quotation. As for his saying "it occurred without following [a noun]", that does not prevent its being an adjective, because when the qualified noun is known it may be omitted with its adjective remaining, as in His saying, Exalted is He: {وَمِنَ الناس والدوآب والأنعام مُخْتَلِفٌ أَلْوَانُهُ} [Fāṭir: 28], i.e. a kind differing [in colours], and as in the poet's saying:
30 - كناطحٍ صخرةً يوماً لِيُوْهِنَها ... فلم يَضِرْها وأَوْهَى قرنَه الوَعِلُ
(Like one who butts a rock one day to weaken it, but does not harm it — the mountain goat only weakened its own horn.)
i.e. like a butting mountain goat; and this is frequent.

«الرحمة», lexically, is tenderness and inclining [towards another]; from it is derived «الرَّحِم» (the womb), which is the belly [Translator's note: the source reads «الابطن», apparently a misprint, perhaps for «البطن» (the belly).], because it inclines over the foetus. On this basis, His being described, Exalted is He, by mercy is a figurative expression (majāz) for His bestowing favours on His servants, like a king who, when he inclines towards his subjects, his good reaches them. This is the meaning of the words of Abū al-Qāsim al-Zamakhsharī. On this supposition it is an attribute of action, not an attribute of essence. It was also said: mercy is willing good for whomever Allah wills that for; on this view describing Him by it is literal (ḥaqīqa), and it is then an attribute of essence. This view is the apparent one.
It was also said: mercy is a tenderness that entails doing good to the one shown mercy; it is used sometimes for mere tenderness and sometimes for mere doing good; when the Creator, Exalted is He, is described by it, nothing is meant but mere doing good, without tenderness. On this basis it is related: "Mercy from Allah is bestowal of favour and bounty, and from human beings it is tenderness and sympathy."
[Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "They are two tender names, one of them more tender than the other," i.e. more abundant in mercy. Al-Khaṭṭābī said: this is problematic, because tenderness] has no place among His attributes. Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl said: "This is an error of the narrator; rather they are two gentle names (rafīqān), one of them gentler than the other, and gentleness (al-rifq) is one of His attributes." And he ﷺ said: "Allah is Gentle and loves gentleness, and gives for it what He does not give for harshness"; and the ḥadīth supports it. As for «الرحيم», it is the One gentle towards the believers in particular.

The scholars differed about «الرحمن الرحيم» as to whether they have one meaning or different meanings.
Some held that they have one meaning, like «نَدْمان» and «نَدِيم» (boon companion). These then differed on two views. Some said: they were combined for emphasis. Others said: when Musaylima — may Allah curse him — named himself «الرحمن», Allah said of Himself: «الرحمنُ الرحيم», so the combination of these two attributes belongs to Allah, Exalted is He, alone. This is very weak, for his naming himself thus counts for nothing at all; and also «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم» preceded the appearance of Musaylima's affair.
Others said: each one has a benefit other than the benefit of the other, and they made this relate to the difference in what each is connected to, since it is said: "Raḥmān of this world and Raḥīm of the Hereafter" — this is related from the Prophet ﷺ — because His mercy in this world embraces believer and unbeliever, while in the Hereafter it is particular to the believers. It is also related: "Raḥīm of this world and Raḥmān of the Hereafter." Distinguishing between them by this measure alone is open to a question that is not hidden.
Others held that the two are different; and these too differed. Some said: «الرحمن» is more intensive, and therefore it is not applied to any but the Creator, Exalted is He. Al-Zamakhsharī chose this and placed it in the category of «غَضْبان» and «سَكْران», for one filled with anger and drunkenness; hence it is said: "Raḥmān of this world and the Hereafter, and Raḥīm of the Hereafter only." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "So the rule would have been to rise from the lower to the higher, as one says «شُجاع باسل» ('brave, intrepid') and does not say «باسِلٌ شجاع»." Then he answered that He followed «الرحمن», which covers the great favours and their roots, with «الرحيم», to be like a completion and a sequel covering the fine and subtle among them.
Others reversed this and made «الرحيم» more intensive. This is supported by the narration of whoever said: "Raḥīm of this world and Ḥamān [sic] of the Hereafter" [Translator's note: «وحمان» in the source is evidently a misprint for «ورحمان».], because in this world He has mercy on believer and unbeliever, while in the Hereafter He has mercy only on the believer. But the correct view is that «الرحمن» is more intensive. As for this narration, there is no proof in it; rather it indicates that «الرحمن» is more intensive, because on the Day of Resurrection mercy is manifold greater and its effect more manifest, according to what is related: that He has stored up for His servants ninety-nine mercies for the Day of Resurrection. The apparent view is that the aspect of intensiveness in the two differs: the intensiveness of faʿlān is from the aspect of fullness and predominance, and the intensiveness of faʿīl is from the aspect of repetition and occurrence at the places of mercy. Abū ʿUbayda said: "The form faʿlān is not like the form faʿīl, for the form faʿlān occurs only for intensiveness of the action, as in «رجل غَضْبانُ», for one filled with anger; while faʿīl may be in the sense of the active and of the passive [participle]." He said:
31 - فأمَّا إذا عَضَّتْ بك الحربُ عَضَّةً ... فإنك مَعْطوفٌ عليك رحيمُ
(But when war bites you with a bite, you are one who is shown sympathy, pitied.)
So «الرحمن» is particular in name and general in action, and «الرحيم» is general in name and particular in action; therefore faʿlān does not take a direct object, while faʿīl does. Ibn Sīdah reported: «زيدٌ حفيظٌ علمَك وعلمَ غيرك» ("Zayd retains your knowledge and the knowledge of others").

The alif and lām in «الرحمن» are for predominance (ghalaba), as in «الصَّعِق». According to most scholars it is not applied to any other than the Creator, Exalted is He, because of His saying, Exalted is He: {قُلِ ادعوا الله أَوِ ادعوا الرحمن} [al-Isrāʾ: 110], where He set it as an equivalent to that in which there is no sharing — unlike «رحيم», which is applied to others than Him, Exalted is He; He [the Exalted] said concerning the Prophet ﷺ:
{بالمؤمنين رؤوف رحيم} [al-Tawba: 128]. As for the saying of the poet about Musaylima the Liar — may Allah the Exalted curse him:
32 - . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . ... وأنت غَيْثُ الوَرى لا زلت رَحْمانا
(And you are the rain [succour] of mankind; may you never cease to be raḥmān.)
no attention is paid to his saying, owing to the excess of their obstinacy. It is used only made definite by the alif and lām or annexed; and no attention is paid to his saying «لا زِلْتَ رَحْمانا», because of its anomaly.
Among the strange things reported about it is that it is Arabicised, not Arabic in origin, and that it is [originally] with the dotted khāʾ; Thaʿlab [and al-Mubarrad] said this, [and he recited]:
33 - لن تُدْرِكوا المَجْدَ أو تَشْرُوا عَباءَكُمُ ... بِالخَزِّ أو تَجْعلوا اليَنْبُوتَ ضَمْرانا
أو تَتْرُكونَ إلى القَسَّيْنِ هِجْرَتَكُمْ ... ومَسْحكم صُلبَهم رَخْمانَ قُرْبانا
(You will not attain glory until you exchange your woollen cloaks for silk, or turn the carob shrub into ḍamrān [a fragrant plant], or abandon your migration to the two priests and your stroking of their cross as an offering to Rakhmān.)

Regarding joining «الرحيم» to «الحمد» there are three ways. The one followed by the majority: «الرحيمِ» with kasra on the mīm, joined to «الحمد». In this kasra there are two possibilities: one — and it is the sounder — that it is a case vowel (ḥarakat iʿrāb); and it was said: it is possible that the mīm was made quiescent with the intention of pausing, and when a quiescent letter came after it, it was vowelled with kasra. The second of the ways of joining: making the mīm quiescent and pausing on it, then beginning with the alif of «الحمد» pronounced as a disjunctive hamza; Umm Salama related this from him ﷺ. The third: al-Kisāʾī reported from some of the Arabs that they recite: «الرحيمَ الحمدُ», with fatḥa on the mīm and joining the alif of «الحمد», as if they made it quiescent and pronounced the alif disjunctively, then treated the pause like continuous speech and threw the vowel of the connective hamza onto the quiescent mīm. Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "This has not been transmitted as a reading from anyone [as far as I know]," and this is open to a question that will come at {الم الله} [Āl ʿImrān: 1-2]. I say: its verification will come in Āl ʿImrān, if Allah the Exalted wills. This admits of another interpretation, namely that the vowel is for the accusative by an omitted verb, by way of qaṭʿ (cutting off [the adjective from its noun]) — and that is preferable to this strained explanation.

ukberi-tibyan:1-1.t:
The I'rab of the Basmala

Allah the Exalted said: (بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ (١))
The bāʾ in بِسْمِ is attached (mutaʿalliq) to something omitted. According to the Basrans, the omitted element is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and the preposition with its genitive noun is its khabar (predicate); the implied wording is "my beginning is بِسْمِ اللَّهِ", i.e. "is (taking place) with the name of Allah"; so the bāʾ is attached to the notion of existence and settledness (al-kawn wa-l-istiqrār).
The Kufans said: the omitted element is a verb, its implied form being "I began" (ابْتَدَأْتُ) or "I begin" (أَبْدَأُ); so the preposition and its genitive noun are in the position of the accusative, governed by the omitted verb. The alif was dropped from the script because of the frequency of use; if you said لِاسْمِ اللَّهِ بَرَكَةٌ ("the name of Allah has blessing") or بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ, you would keep the alif in writing.
It is also said that they dropped the alif because they treated it as سِمٌ, which is a dialectal variant of اسْمٌ.
Its dialectal forms are five: سِمٌ with kasra on the sīn and with ḍamma; اسْمٌ with kasra on the hamza and with ḍamma; and سُمًى, like ضُحًى.
The original form of اسْمٌ is سُمُوٌ, so what has been dropped from it is its final radical (lām). This is shown by their saying in its plural أَسْمَاءُ and أَسَامِي, and in its diminutive «سُمَيٌّ»; and they formed from it the pattern faʿīl, saying فُلَانٌ سَمِيُّكَ, i.e. "his name is like your name"; and the verb from it is سَمَّيْتُ and أَسْمَيْتُ. So you have seen how the dropped letter returned at its end.
The Kufans said: its origin is وَسَمَ, because it is from al-wasm, which is "the mark". This is correct in meaning but unsound as a derivation.
If it is asked: how is the noun "name" put in a genitive construct with "Allah", when "Allah" is itself the name?
It is answered in three ways. First: "name" here means "naming" (al-tasmiya), and naming is other than the name, because the name is what adheres to the one named, while naming is uttering the name.
Second: there is an omitted muḍāf in the phrase, its implied form being "with the name of the one named Allah".
Third: that اسْمٌ is redundant (zāʾid). Of this kind is the saying of the poet:
إِلَى الْحَوْلِ ثُمَّ اسْمُ السَّلَامِ عَلَيْكُمَا
("Until the year is out; then the name of peace be upon you both")
and the saying of another:
دَاعٍ يُنَادِيهِ بِاسْمِ الْمَاءِ
("A caller calling it by the name of water")
meaning "peace be upon you both" and "we call it with 'water'".
The original form of اللَّهِ is الْإِلَاءُ [Translator's note: so in the text; the intended form is evidently الْإِلَاهُ]. The vowel of the hamza was thrown onto the lām of definiteness; then it [the lām] was made quiescent and assimilated into the second lām. Then it was pronounced heavy (velarised) when no kasra precedes it, [and light when a kasra precedes it]; and some pronounce it light in every case. The heavy pronunciation in this noun is one of its special properties.
Abū ʿAlī said: the hamza of إِلَاهٌ was dropped outright, without throwing its vowel onto the preceding letter; and the hamza of إِلَاهٌ is a radical. It is from أَلِهَ يَأْلَهُ, said when one is worshipped; so الْإِلَهُ is a maṣdar (verbal noun) standing in the place of the passive participle, i.e. الْمَأْلُوهُ, which is "the one worshipped".
It is also said that the hamza was originally a wāw, because it is from al-walah; so الْإِلَهُ is the one towards whom hearts are bewildered (tawallahu), i.e. become perplexed.
It is also said that its origin is لَاهُ on the pattern faʿil, and that the original of the alif is yāʾ, because in its metathesised form they said لَهِيَ أَبُوكَ; then the alif and lām were prefixed to it.
(الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ): two adjectives derived from al-raḥma (mercy).
الرَّحْمَنُ is one of the patterns of intensiveness, and there is intensiveness in الرَّحِيمُ as well, except that faʿlān is more intensive than faʿīl.
Their genitive is as adjectives (ṣifa), and what governs the adjective is what governs the noun it describes.
Al-Akhfash said: what governs it is abstract (maʿnawī), namely its being a follower. It is permissible to put both in the accusative by implying أَعْنِي ("I mean"), and in the nominative by implying هُوَ ("He is").

ukberi-tibyan:2-3.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ (٢) الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ (٣))
The majority read (الْحَمْدُ) in the nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and (لِلَّهِ) is the khabar (predicate); the lām is attached (mutaʿalliq) to something omitted, i.e. "is due" or "is established". (الْحَمْدُ) is also read in the accusative, as the maṣdar (verbal noun) of an omitted verb, i.e. "I praise with praise" (أَحْمَدُ الْحَمْدَ). The nominative is better, because it carries generality in meaning.
It is also read with kasra on the dāl, in harmony with the kasra of the lām, just as they said الْمِعِيرَةُ and رِغِيفٌ. This is weak in the verse, because in it the declensional ending is made to follow an indeclinable (mabnī) ending, and that amounts to cancelling the declension.
It is also read with ḍamma on both the dāl and the lām, making the lām follow the dāl. This too is weak, because the lām of the genitive is joined to what comes after it and separate from the dāl, and there is no parallel to it among the single-letter prepositions. However, whoever read it this way was fleeing from passing from a ḍamma to a kasra, and treated it as though it were joined, since الْحَمْدُ is hardly ever used detached from what follows it.
(رَبِّ) is the maṣdar of رَبَّ يَرُبُّ, then made into an adjective, like عَدْلٌ and خَصْمٌ; its original form is رَابَ [Translator's note: i.e. the active participle رَابٌّ].
Its genitive is as an adjective (ṣifa) or a badal (substitute). It has been read in the accusative by implying أَعْنِي ("I mean"); and it is said: as a vocative. It has been read in the nominative by implying هُوَ ("He is").
(الْعَالَمِينَ) is a sound plural; its singular is عَالَمٌ. الْعَالَمُ is a noun coined for a plurality and has no singular from its own wording. Its derivation is from al-ʿilm (knowledge) for those who restrict الْعَالَمُ to rational beings, or from al-ʿalāma (sign) for those who make it cover all created things.
In (الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ) the genitive, the accusative and the nominative are possible, and each has been read, as we mentioned for رَبّ.

ukberi-tibyan:4-4.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ (٤))
His saying, the Exalted: مَالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ is read with kasra on the lām without an alif (مَلِكِ); this is one whose dominion (mulk) is established; one says "a king (مَلِكٌ) evident in kingship (الْمُلْكِ)", with ḍamma. It has also been read with the lām quiescent (مَلْكِ); this is a lightening of the form with kasra, like فَخِذٌ and كَتِفٌ. On this reading its genitive construct is pure (maḥḍa) and it is definite, so its genitive is as an adjective (ṣifa) or a badal (substitute) for اللَّهِ, and on this reading there is no omission in it.
It is also read with the alif and in the genitive (مَالِكِ); on this reading it is indefinite, because the active participle, when present or future time is intended by it, does not become definite through the genitive construct. On this reading its genitive is as a badal, not as an adjective, because a definite noun is not described by an indefinite one. In the phrase there is an omitted object, its implied form being "Owner of the affair of the Day of Judgement" (مَالِكِ أَمْرِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ), or "Owner, on the Day of Judgement, of the affair" (مَالِكِ يَوْمَ الدِّينِ الْأَمْرَ). Through being put in the genitive construct with «يَوْمِ» it has left the adverbial status, because implying «فِي» in it is not valid, since that would separate the muḍāf from the muḍāf ilayhi.
مَالِكَ is also read in the accusative, either by implying أَعْنِي ("I mean"), or as a ḥāl (circumstantial).
Some have allowed it to be a vocative. It is also read in the nominative by implying هُوَ ("He is"), or as a khabar (predicate) for الرَّحْمَنُ الرَّحِيمُ on the reading of those who put الرَّحْمَنُ in the nominative. It is also read مَلِيكُ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ, in the nominative, the accusative and the genitive.
It is also read (مَلَكَ يَوْمَ الدِّينِ), as a verb, with يَوْمَ as its object or as an adverbial (ẓarf). (الدِّينُ) is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of دَانَ يَدِينُ.

ukberi-tibyan:5-5.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وَإِيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ (٥))
His saying, the Exalted: (إِيَّاكَ): the majority read it with kasra on the hamza and a doubled yāʾ.
It has been read, as an irregular (shādhdh) reading, with fatḥa on the hamza (أَيَّاكَ); the more likely view is that this is a dialectal form heard from the Arabs.
It has also been read with kasra on the hamza and a single, undoubled yāʾ (إِيَاكَ). The explanation of this is that one of the two yāʾs was dropped because repetition in a weak letter is felt heavy. This has occurred in poetry; al-Farazdaq said:
تَنَظَّرْتُ نَصْرًا وَالسِّمَاكَيْنِ أَيْهُمَا ... عَلَيَّ مَعَ الْغَيْثِ اسْتَهَلَّتْ مَوَاطِرُهُ
("I watched Naṣr and the two Simāks [stars], [to see] which of the two would pour its rains upon me with the downpour")
And they said in أَمَّا: أَيْمَا, turning the mīm into a yāʾ out of dislike for the doubling.
According to al-Khalīl and Sībawayh, إِيَّا is a pronoun noun. As for the kāf, according to Sībawayh it is a particle of address that has no grammatical position, and it cannot be a noun, because if it were a noun, إِيَّا would be in a genitive construct with it, and pronouns are not put in a genitive construct. According to al-Khalīl it is a pronoun noun to which إِيَّا is put in a genitive construct, because إِيَّا resembles the overt noun in its coming before the verb and the agent, and in its length through its many letters. It is reported from the Arabs: "When a man reaches sixty, then [let him beware of] himself and of the young women" (إِذَا بَلَغَ الرَّجُلُ السِّتِّينَ فَإِيَّاهُ وَإِيَّا الشَّوَابِّ).
The Kufans said: إِيَّاكَ in its entirety [is the pronoun]. This is far-fetched, because the end of this noun differs according to the difference between speaker, addressee and absent person, so one says إِيَّايَ, إِيَّاكَ and إِيَّاهُ.
Some said: the kāf is the noun, and إِيَّا is a support (ʿimād) for it, and it is a particle. The position of إِيَّاكَ is accusative, governed by (نَعْبُدُ).
If it is asked: إِيَّاكَ is in the second person, while الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ is in the wording of the third person, so it would have been more consistent for it to be إِيَّاهُ —
it is answered: it is the habit of the Arabs to turn from the third person to the second, and from the second person to the third, and you will come across a good number of such cases in the Qur'an.
His saying, the Exalted: (نَسْتَعِينُ): the majority read it with fatḥa on the nūn; it has also been read with kasra on it (نِسْتَعِينُ), and that is a dialectal form. Its original form is نَسْتَعْوِنُ, the pattern nastafʿilu from al-ʿawn (help). The kasra was felt heavy on the wāw, so it was transferred to the ʿayn; then the wāw was turned into a yāʾ because it was quiescent and the letter before it had a kasra.

ukberi-tibyan:6-7.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ (٦) صِرَاطَ الَّذِينَ أَنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ).
His saying, the Exalted: (اهْدِنَا): its form is an imperative. The imperative is indeclinable (mabnī) on sukūn according to the Basrans, and declinable according to the Kufans. So the dropping of the yāʾ, according to the Basrans, is the sign of the sukūn which is its indeclinable ending, and according to the Kufans it is the sign of the jussive (jazm).
(هَدَى) is transitive to one object by itself. As for its transitivity to a second object, it has come transitive to it by itself, and of this kind is this verse; it has come transitive with إِلَى, as in His saying, the Exalted: (هَدَانِي رَبِّي إِلَى صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ); and it has come transitive with the lām, and of this kind is His saying, the Exalted: (الَّذِي هَدَانَا لِهَذَا).
(السِّرَاطَ) with sīn is the original form, because it is from سَرَطَ الشَّيْءَ, said when one "reaches" (بَلَغَهُ) a thing [Translator's note: so in the text; the comparison with "a thing swallowed" that follows suggests بَلَعَهُ, "swallowed it"]. The road was called سِرَاطٌ because people flow along it as a swallowed thing flows.
So whoever read it with sīn brought it in its original form; and whoever read it with ṣād turned the sīn into ṣād to make it homogeneous with the ṭāʾ in velarisation (iṭbāq). The sīn shares with the ṣād the qualities of whistling (ṣafīr) and whispering (hams); since it shares these with the ṣād it is close to it, and its closeness to it permitted turning it into ṣād so as to make it homogeneous with the ṭāʾ in velarisation.
Whoever read it with zāy turned the sīn into zāy, because the zāy and the sīn are both whistling letters, and the zāy is more like the ṭāʾ, because both are voiced (majhūr).
Whoever gave the ṣād a tinge of zāy (ishmām) intended to place it between voicing and velarisation.
The original form of (الْمُسْتَقِيمَ) is مُسْتَقْوِمٌ; then the same was done to it as we mentioned in «نَسْتَعِينُ». The pattern mustafʿil here has the meaning of faʿīl, i.e. "the upright (الْقَوِيمُ) path". It may also mean الْقَائِمُ, i.e. "the established, firm".
The second صِرَاطَ is a badal (substitute) for the first; it is the substitution of a thing for the thing itself (badal al-shayʾ min al-shayʾ), both having one meaning, and both are definite.
(الَّذِينَ) is a relative noun; its ṣila (relative clause) is أَنْعَمْتَ, and what refers back to it is the hāʾ and the mīm [in عَلَيْهِمْ].
The purpose of coining «الَّذِي» is to describe definite nouns by clauses, because clauses are interpreted as indefinites, and a definite noun cannot be described by an indefinite. The alif and lām in الَّذِي are redundant (zāʾid), and its definiteness comes from the ṣila. Do you not see that مَنْ and مَا are definite though they contain no lām? This shows that their definiteness is through the ṣila. The original form of الَّذِينَ is اللَّذِيُونَ, because its singular is الَّذِي; but the yāʾ of the plural caused the original yāʾ to be dropped, so that two quiescent letters would not meet.
الَّذِينَ is with yāʾ in every case, because it is an indeclinable (mabnī) noun. Some of the Arabs make it with wāw in the nominative and with yāʾ in the genitive and accusative, just as they made its dual with alif in the nominative and with yāʾ in the genitive and accusative.
In الَّذِي there are five dialectal forms. First: لَذِي, with a lām with fatḥa, without the lām of definiteness; it has been read so as an irregular (shādhdh) reading. Second: الَّذِي with the yāʾ quiescent. Third: dropping the yāʾ and keeping the kasra of the dhāl. Fourth: dropping the yāʾ and making the dhāl quiescent. Fifth: with a doubled yāʾ.

ukberi-tibyan:7-7.t:
Allah the Exalted said: (غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ)
His saying, the Exalted: (غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ) is read in the genitive, and there are three views on it. First: it is a badal (substitute) for الَّذِينَ. Second: it is a badal for the hāʾ and mīm in عَلَيْهِمْ. Third: it is a naʿt (adjective) of الَّذِينَ.
If you say: الَّذِينَ is definite, and «غَيْرُ» does not become definite through the genitive construct, so it cannot validly be an adjective of it — there are two answers. First: «غَيْرُ», when it falls between two opposites that are both definite, becomes definite through the genitive construct, as in your saying عَجِبْتُ مِنَ الْحَرَكَةِ غَيْرِ السُّكُونِ ("I marvelled at the motion that is other than rest"); and so it is here, because the one favoured and the one with whom [Allah] is angry are two opposites. The second answer: الَّذِينَ is close to an indefinite, because no particular people are intended by it; and غَيْرِ الْمَغْضُوبِ is close to a definite through the specification it gains from the genitive construct. So each of the two has vagueness in one respect and specificity in another.
(غَيْرَ) is also read in the accusative, and there are three views on it. First: it is a ḥāl (circumstantial) from the hāʾ and mīm, and what governs it is أَنْعَمْتَ. It is weak for it to be a ḥāl from الَّذِينَ, because that is a muḍāf ilayhi, and الصِّرَاطَ cannot by itself govern the ḥāl. It has also been said that it is accusative as a ḥāl from الَّذِينَ, governed by the meaning of the genitive construct. The second view: it is accusative as an exception (istithnāʾ) from الَّذِينَ, or from the hāʾ and mīm. The third: it is accusative by implying أَعْنِي ("I mean").
(الْمَغْضُوبِ) is a passive participle from غَضِبَ عَلَيْهِ, which is intransitive; what stands in the place of the agent is «عَلَيْهِمْ». The implied wording is "other than the group with whom [Allah] is angry" (غَيْرُ الْفَرِيقِ الْمَغْضُوبِ). There is no pronoun in الْمَغْضُوبِ, because the preposition with its genitive noun stands in the place of the agent; for this reason it is not pluralised, so that one would say الْفَرِيقُ الْمَغْضُوبِينَ عَلَيْهِمْ, because the active and passive participle, when it governs what follows it, is not given the sound plural.
(وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ): (لَا) is redundant (zāʾida) for emphasis according to the Basrans. According to the Kufans it has the meaning of غَيْرَ, as they said جِئْتُ بِلَا شَيْءٍ ("I came with no-thing"), putting a preposition before it, so that it takes the status of غَيْرَ.
The Basrans answered this by saying that (لَا) entered for the sake of meaning, so the governing word stepped over it, just as it steps over the alif and lām. The majority read الضَّالِّينَ without hamza; Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī read it with a hamza with fatḥa (الضَّأَلِّينَ). This is a dialectal form widespread among the Arabs in every alif followed by a doubled letter, such as ضَالٌّ, دَابَّةٌ and جَانٌّ. The reason for this is that he turned the alif into a hamza so that it could validly bear a vowel, so that two quiescent letters would not be combined.

Section: As for (آمِينَ), it is a verbal noun (ism fiʿl), and its meaning is "O Allah, answer". It is indeclinable (mabnī) because it occurs in the place of an indeclinable word [the imperative]. It was given the fatḥa because of the yāʾ before its last letter, just as أَيْنَ was given fatḥa; and the fatḥa is stronger in it [than in أَيْنَ], because there is a kasra before the yāʾ, so if the nūn were given kasra according to the basic rule, the yāʾ would fall between two kasras.
It has been said that (آمِينَ) is one of the names of Allah the Exalted, its implied form being يَا آمِينَ ("O Āmīn"). This is a mistake for two reasons. First: the names of Allah are known only by being received through transmission, and no transmitted text has come with that.
Second: if it were so, it would be indeclinable on ḍamma, because it would be a vocative that is definite or specifically intended. There are two dialectal forms of it: the short form (أَمِينَ), which is the original, and the long form (آمِينَ), which is not one of the Arabic patterns, but rather one of the foreign patterns, like هَابِيلُ and قَابِيلُ. The explanation of it is that the fatḥa of the hamza was lengthened, so that the alif arose; on this account it does not leave the Arabic patterns.

Section on the hāʾ of the pronoun, as in عَلَيْهِمْ, عَلَيْهِ, فِيهِ and فِيهِمْ.
We have treated it separately only because it recurs in the Qur'an. The original vowel of this hāʾ is ḍamma, because it takes ḍamma after fatḥa, after ḍamma and after sukūn, as in إِنَّهُ, لَهُ, غُلَامُهُ, يَسْمَعُهُ and مِنْهُ. Its kasra is permitted only after yāʾ, as in عَلَيْهِمْ and أَيْدِيهِمْ, and after kasra, as in بِهِ and بِدَارِهِ. Giving it ḍamma in both of these places is permitted, because that is the original; it was given kasra only to make it homogeneous with the yāʾ or kasra before it. Each of these has been read.
As for (عَلَيْهِمْ), there are ten dialectal forms in it, and all have been read: five with ḍamma on the hāʾ and five with kasra on it.
Those with ḍamma [on the hāʾ]: making the mīm quiescent; giving it ḍamma without lengthening; giving it ḍamma with a wāw; giving the mīm kasra without a yāʾ; and giving it kasra with a yāʾ. As for those with kasra on the hāʾ: making the mīm quiescent; giving it kasra without a yāʾ; giving it kasra with a yāʾ; giving it ḍamma without a wāw; and giving it ḍamma with a wāw.
The original state of the mīm of the plural is that a wāw follows it, as Ibn Kathīr read. The mīm is for going beyond the singular; the alif is the sign of the dual, as in عَلَيْهِمَا; and the wāw is for the plural, the counterpart of the alif. What shows this is that the sign of the plural in the feminine is a doubled nūn, as in عَلَيْهِنَّ; so likewise the sign of the masculine plural must be two letters. However, they dropped the wāw for lightness, and there is no ambiguity in that, because the singular has no mīm, and the dual has an alif after its mīm. When the wāw is dropped, the mīm becomes quiescent, so that vowels do not follow one another in most places, as in ضَرْبِهِمْ and يَضْرِبُهُمْ.
So whoever kept the wāw, or dropped it and made the mīm quiescent, did so for the reasons we mentioned. Whoever gave the mīm ḍamma indicated thereby that its original vowel is ḍamma, and made the ḍamma an indication of the dropped wāw.
Whoever gave the mīm kasra and followed it with a yāʾ gave the mīm the vowel of the hāʾ with kasra before it, then turned the wāw into a yāʾ because it was quiescent and the letter before it had a kasra.
Whoever dropped the yāʾ made the kasra an indication of it.
Whoever gave the mīm kasra after a ḍamma on the hāʾ intended thereby to make it homogeneous with the yāʾ that comes before the hāʾ.
Whoever gave the hāʾ ḍamma said: the yāʾ in عَلَيْهَا by right should be an alif, just as the alif remains with an overt noun [عَلَى زَيْدٍ], and the yāʾ is not the original of the alif; so just as the hāʾ takes ḍamma after an alif, it likewise takes ḍamma after the yāʾ substituted for it.
Whoever gave the hāʾ kasra took account of the pronunciation. As for giving the hāʾ kasra and following it with a quiescent yāʾ, that is permitted though weak. It is permitted because the hāʾ, being faint, is made clear by lengthening; it is weak because the hāʾ is faint, and the faint is close to the quiescent, and the quiescent is not a solid barrier, so it is as though the yāʾ were adjacent to the yāʾ.
When the mīm meets a quiescent letter after it, it may take ḍamma, as in عَلَيْهِمُ الذِّلَّةُ, because its original vowel is ḍamma and it was made quiescent only for lightness; so when a vowel is needed on it, the ḍamma, which is its due originally, is more appropriate. It may also take kasra, in harmony with what precedes it.
As for فِيهِ and بَنِيهِ, they admit kasra without lengthening and with lengthening, and ḍamma without lengthening and with lengthening.
As for when the letter before the hāʾ is quiescent, as in مِنْهُ, عَنْهُ and تَجِدُوهُ: whoever gave it ḍamma without lengthening followed the original; and whoever lengthened it intended to make the hāʾ clear because of its faintness.

zajjaj:1-1.t:
بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ
Abū Isḥāq Ibrāhīm ibn al-Sarī al-Zajjāj said: This is an abridged book on the i'rab (grammatical analysis) of the Qur'an and its meanings; and we ask Allah for success in all matters.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾: What brings in the bāʾ is the meaning of beginning, as though you said: "بَدَأْتُ بِاسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ" (I begin with the name of Allah, the All-Merciful, the Most Merciful), except that there was no need to mention "بَدَأْتُ", because the situation (al-ḥāl) shows that you are beginning. The alif dropped from "بِاسْمِ اللَّهِ" in pronunciation, the original being "بِاسْمِ اللَّهِ", because it is a connecting alif (alif waṣl), which was brought in to make it possible to pronounce the vowelless letter. The proof of this is that when you form the diminutive of اسم you say "سُمَيٌّ". The Arabs say: "هَذا اِسْمٌ", "هَذا اُسْمٌ" and "هَذا سِمٌ". The rajaz poet said:
بِاسْمِ الَّذِي في كُلِّ سُورَةٍ سِمُهُ
(In the name of the One whose name is in every sura.)
— and "سُمُهُ" as well; Abū Zayd al-Anṣārī and other grammarians transmitted this. So the alif dropped for the reason we mentioned. Likewise your saying "اِبْنٌ": the alif in it is a connecting alif; you say in its diminutive "بُنَيٌّ". The meaning of our word "اِسْمٌ" is that it is derived from "اَلسُّمُوُّ", and "اَلسُّمُوُّ" is elevation. Its origin is "سَمَوٌ", with wāw, on the pattern of "جَمَلٌ", and its plural is "أسْماءٌ", like "قِنْوٌ" / "أقْناءٌ" and "حَنْوٌ" / "أحْناءٌ". The name (ism) was made only as an exalting of the meaning by the name of Allah, because the meaning lies beneath the name.

Whoever says that اسم is taken from "وَسَمْتُ" (I marked) is mistaken, because we know of nothing that a connecting alif has entered and whose fāʾ — I mean the fāʾ of the verb (the first radical) — has been dropped, as in your saying "عِدَةٌ" and "زِنَةٌ", whose origin is "وَعْدَةٌ" and "وَزْنَةٌ". If "اِسْمٌ" were "وَسْمَةٌ", its diminutive, once the connecting alif is dropped from it, would be "وُسَيْمٌ", just as the diminutive of "عِدَّةٌ" and "صِلَةٌ" is "وُعَيْدَةٌ" and "وُصَيْلَةٌ". No one can show a connecting alif in any noun whose fāʾ has been dropped. The alif dropped in writing from "بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ" but did not drop in ﴿اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ﴾ [al-ʿAlaq: 1], because in it (the basmala) there combined — together with its dropping in pronunciation — frequency of use.

Sībawayh held that the meaning of the bāʾ is attachment (ilṣāq). You say: "كَتَبْتُ بِالقَلَمِ" (I wrote with the pen), the meaning being that the writing is attached to the pen. It is always vowelled with kasra, because it has no meaning other than the genitive (khafḍ), so its pronunciation had to be with kasra, to distinguish between what puts into the genitive while being a noun — like the kāf in your saying "كَزَيْدٍ" — and what puts into the genitive while being a particle — like "بِزَيْدٍ". For the basic vowel of the particles that are spoken and consist of a single letter is always fatḥa, unless some cause comes along that removes it, because a single letter has no share in inflection (iʿrāb); but it occurs at the beginning of speech, and one cannot begin with a vowelless letter, so fatḥa was chosen, because it is the lightest of the vowels. You say: "رَأيْتُ زَيْدًا وعَمْرًا", and the wāw has fatḥa; likewise "فَعَمْرًا": the fāʾ has fatḥa. The lām was given kasra in your saying "لِزَيْدٍ" only to distinguish between the lām of the oath and the lām of annexation (lām al-iḍāfa). Do you not see that if you said "إنَّ هَذا لِزَيْدٍ" (this belongs to Zayd), it would be known that it is his property, and if you said "إنَّ هَذا لَزَيْدٌ" (this is indeed Zayd), it would be known that the one pointed at is Zayd? That is why the lām was given kasra in your saying "لِزَيْدٍ". If you said "إنَّ هَذا المالَ لَكَ" and "إنَّ هَذا لَأنْتَ", you would give the lām fatḥa, because the ambiguity has gone.

What we have said about the lām is the doctrine of Sībawayh, Yūnus, al-Khalīl, Abū ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAlāʾ and all the grammarians whose knowledge is trusted. Likewise you say "أزَيْدٌ في الدّارِ؟" (Is Zayd in the house?), and the alif (hamza) has fatḥa. Among the initial particles consisting of a single letter there is no letter with kasra except the bāʾ and the lām of command alone, and they were given kasra only for the cause we mentioned; and likewise the lām of annexation, whose basic vowel is fatḥa. As for the lām of "كَيْ" in your saying "جِئْتُ لِتَقُومَ يا هَذا" (I came so that you would stand, O you), it is the lām of annexation that is in your saying "اَلْمالُ لِزَيْدٍ" (the property belongs to Zayd); "تَقُومَ" is put in the accusative only by an implied "أنْ", or by "كَيْ" which has the meaning of "أنْ"; so the meaning is: "جِئْتُ لِقِيامِكَ" (I came for your standing). What we have said on the derivation of "اِسْمٌ" is a view that we know no one explained before us.

As for your saying "لِيَضْرِبْ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا" (let Zayd strike ʿAmr), the lām was given kasra only to differentiate it from the lām of emphasis (tawkīd); its resemblance to the lām of the genitive does not matter, because the lām of the genitive does not occur with verbs, whereas the lām of emphasis does occur with verbs. Do you not see that if you said "لَتَضْرِبْ" while commanding, it would resemble the lām of emphasis when you say "إنَّكَ لَتَضْرِبُ" (you indeed strike)? This is the sum of what there is concerning the particles that consist of a single letter. As for the name of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, the alif in it is a connecting alif; and I dislike mentioning everything the grammarians have said about the name of Allah — I mean our saying "اللَّهِ" — out of reverence for Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 3]: these are attributes of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. Their meaning, according to what Abū ʿUbayda mentioned, is: "the Possessor of mercy". It is not permissible to say "اَلرَّحْمَنُ" of anyone but Allah. That is only because the pattern "فَعْلانُ" is among the patterns of what is described intensively. Do you not see that when you say "غَضْبانُ", its meaning is "the one filled with anger"? So "رَحْمَنُ" is the One whose mercy encompasses everything; hence it is not permissible to call anyone other than Allah "رَحْمَنُ". These attributes were put in the genitive because they are praise of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, so their i'rab is the i'rab of His name. If you said — outside the Qur'an — "بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الكَرِيمَ" and "اَلْكَرِيمُ", and "اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبَّ العالَمِينَ" and "رَبُّ العالَمِينَ", that would be permissible. Whoever puts "رَبَّ العالَمِينَ" in the accusative does so only because it is praise of Allah: as though, when he said "اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ", it was inferred from this wording that he is mentioning Allah, so his saying "رَبَّ العالَمِينَ" is as though he said "أذْكُرُ رَبَّ العالَمِينَ" (I mention the Lord of the worlds). And when he says "رَبُّ العالَمِينَ", it is on the pattern of your saying "هو رَبُّ العالَمِينَ" (He is the Lord of the worlds). The poet said:
وَكُلُّ قَوْمٍ أطاعُوا أمْرَ مُرْشِدِهِمْ ∗∗∗ إلّا نُمَيْرًا أطاعَتْ أمْرَ غاوِيها
اَلظّاعِنِينَ ولَمّا يُظْعِنُوا أحَدًا ∗∗∗ والقائِلِينَ لِمَن دارٌ نُخَلِّيها
(Every tribe obeyed the command of its right guide, except Numayr, which obeyed the command of the one who led it astray — those who depart though they have made no one depart, and who say: "For whom is a home that we shall vacate?")
So "اَلظّاعِنِينَ" may be put in the accusative in two ways: as following "نُمَيْرًا", and as dispraise (dhamm), as though he said "أذْكُرُ الظّاعِنِينَ" (I mention those who depart). You may also put it in the nominative, meaning "هُمُ الظّاعِنُونَ" (they are those who depart). Likewise in "اَلْقائِلِينَ" you have the accusative and the nominative: you may put both in the nominative, you may put both in the accusative, you may put the first in the nominative and the second in the accusative, and you may put the first in the accusative and the second in the nominative. There is no disagreement among the grammarians about what we have described.

And from Sūrat "al-Ḥamd"
﷽
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾: the meaning of "اَلْحَمْدُ" is thanks and praise of Allah the Exalted. ﴿الحَمْدُ﴾ is in the nominative by being the mubtadaʾ (subject; ibtidāʾ), and His saying ﴿لِلَّهِ﴾ is a predication about al-ḥamd. The preferred form in ordinary speech is the nominative. As for the Qur'an, ﴿الحَمْدُ﴾ is read in it only in the nominative, because the Sunna is followed in the Qur'an, and no attention is paid in it to anything other than the sound transmission which the readers renowned for precision and reliability have read; and the nominative is the reading. In ordinary speech it is permissible to say "اَلْحَمْدَ", meaning "أحْمَدُ اللَّهَ الحَمْدَ" (I praise Allah with praise), dispensing with mention of "أحْمَدُ" because the state of praise is the one creatures ought to be in; but the nominative is better and more eloquent in praising Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. It has been transmitted from some people among the Arabs: "اَلْحَمْدَ لِلَّهِ" and "اَلْحَمْدِ لِلَّهِ"; this is the dialect of people who are paid no attention, and with whose transmission one does not occupy oneself. We have occupied ourselves with transmitting this form only to warn people against using it, or lest an ignorant person think that it is permissible in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, or in speech. Nothing analogous to it has come in the speech of the Arabs, and there is no justification for it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾: we have already explained that in the Qur'an only ﴿رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ﴿الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 3] is permissible, even though the nominative and the accusative are permissible in ordinary speech; for the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, only the best and most eloquent wording is chosen.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿العالَمِينَ﴾: its meaning is everything that Allah created, as He said: "وَهو رَبُّ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ" (and He is the Lord of everything). It is the plural of "عالَمٌ"; you say "هَؤُلاءِ عالَمُونَ" and "رَأيْتُ عالَمِينَ". "عالَمٌ" has no singular from its own root-form, because "عالَمٌ" is a collective for different things; and if "عالَمٌ" is used for one of them, it becomes a plural for similar things. The nūn in "اَلْعالَمِينَ" was given fatḥa because it is the nūn of the plural. Sībawayh held that it was given fatḥa to distinguish it from the nūn of the dual: you say "هَذانِ عالَمانِ يا هَذا", giving the nūn of the dual kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters — and this is explained in its place, if Allah wills. Likewise the nūn of the plural was vowelled with fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and was not given kasra because kasra is heavy after wāw and yāʾ. Do you not see that you say "سَوْفَ أفْعَلُ", giving the fāʾ of "سَوْفَ" fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and not kasra because kasra is heavy after wāw? Likewise you say "أيْنَ زَيْدٌ؟", giving the nūn fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters after yāʾ.

zajjaj:2-2.t:
And from Sūrat "al-Ḥamd"
﷽
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾: the meaning of "اَلْحَمْدُ" is thanks and praise of Allah the Exalted. ﴿الحَمْدُ﴾ is in the nominative by being the mubtadaʾ (subject; ibtidāʾ), and His saying ﴿لِلَّهِ﴾ is a predication about al-ḥamd. The preferred form in ordinary speech is the nominative. As for the Qur'an, ﴿الحَمْدُ﴾ is read in it only in the nominative, because the Sunna is followed in the Qur'an, and no attention is paid in it to anything other than the sound transmission which the readers renowned for precision and reliability have read; and the nominative is the reading. In ordinary speech it is permissible to say "اَلْحَمْدَ", meaning "أحْمَدُ اللَّهَ الحَمْدَ" (I praise Allah with praise), dispensing with mention of "أحْمَدُ" because the state of praise is the one creatures ought to be in; but the nominative is better and more eloquent in praising Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He. It has been transmitted from some people among the Arabs: "اَلْحَمْدَ لِلَّهِ" and "اَلْحَمْدِ لِلَّهِ"; this is the dialect of people who are paid no attention, and with whose transmission one does not occupy oneself. We have occupied ourselves with transmitting this form only to warn people against using it, or lest an ignorant person think that it is permissible in the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, or in speech. Nothing analogous to it has come in the speech of the Arabs, and there is no justification for it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾: we have already explained that in the Qur'an only ﴿رَبِّ العالَمِينَ﴾ ﴿الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 3] is permissible, even though the nominative and the accusative are permissible in ordinary speech; for the Book of Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, only the best and most eloquent wording is chosen.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿العالَمِينَ﴾: its meaning is everything that Allah created, as He said: "وَهو رَبُّ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ" (and He is the Lord of everything). It is the plural of "عالَمٌ"; you say "هَؤُلاءِ عالَمُونَ" and "رَأيْتُ عالَمِينَ". "عالَمٌ" has no singular from its own root-form, because "عالَمٌ" is a collective for different things; and if "عالَمٌ" is used for one of them, it becomes a plural for similar things. The nūn in "اَلْعالَمِينَ" was given fatḥa because it is the nūn of the plural. Sībawayh held that it was given fatḥa to distinguish it from the nūn of the dual: you say "هَذانِ عالَمانِ يا هَذا", giving the nūn of the dual kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters — and this is explained in its place, if Allah wills. Likewise the nūn of the plural was vowelled with fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and was not given kasra because kasra is heavy after wāw and yāʾ. Do you not see that you say "سَوْفَ أفْعَلُ", giving the fāʾ of "سَوْفَ" fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and not kasra because kasra is heavy after wāw? Likewise you say "أيْنَ زَيْدٌ؟", giving the nūn fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters after yāʾ.

zajjaj:4-4.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿مالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾: the reading is the genitive (khafḍ), following the course of "اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ مالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ". If it were put in the accusative — in ordinary speech — on the same basis on which "رَبَّ العالَمِينَ" and "اَلرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ" are put in the accusative, it would be permissible in speech; but in recitation I do not consider it good. In ordinary speech it is also possible to put "رَبِّ العالَمِينَ" and "مالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ" in the accusative as a vocative (nidāʾ), as you say: "اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ يا رَبَّ العالَمِينَ، ويا مالِكَ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ" (Praise be to Allah, O Lord of the worlds and O Master of the Day of Judgement), as though, after saying "اَلْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ", you said: "لَكَ الحَمْدُ يا رَبَّ العالَمِينَ، ويا مالِكَ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ" (To You belongs praise, O Lord of the worlds and O Master of the Day of Judgement). It has been read "مَلِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ" and "مالِكَ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ". The Day of Judgement was singled out — while Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, owns everything — only because it is the day on which created beings are compelled to recognise that the whole command belongs to Allah. Do you not see Him saying: "لِمَنِ المُلْكُ اليَوْمَ" (To whom belongs the dominion this day?), and His saying: "يَوْمَ لا تَمْلِكَ نَفْسٌ لِنَفْسٍ شَيْئًا" (the day when no soul will have power to do anything for another soul)? «[Translator's note: the text as printed vowels the verb تَمْلِكَ with fatḥa; in the Qur'anic text (al-Infiṭār 82:19) it is تَمْلِكُ.]» So it is the day on which no one has power to bring benefit or harm to himself or to anyone else.

Whoever reads ﴿مالِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾ does so in line with His saying: "لِمَنِ المُلْكُ اليَوْمَ", which is equivalent to: "مَنِ المالِكُ اليَوْمَ؟" (Who is the owner this day?). Whoever reads "مَلِكِ يَوْمِ الدِّينِ" does so with the meaning "the One who possesses sovereignty on the Day of Judgement"; and it is said that it is the reading of the Prophet ﷺ.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿يَوْمِ الدِّينِ﴾: "اَلدِّينُ" in the language is recompense. It is said: "كَما تَدِينُ تُدانُ" (as you deal, so you will be dealt with); the meaning is: as you act, so you will be given and recompensed. The poet said:
واعْلَمْ وأيْقِنْ أنَّ مُلْكَكَ زائِلٌ ∗∗∗ واعْلَمْ بِأنَّ كَما تَدِينُ تُدانُ
(Know and be certain that your dominion will pass away, and know that as you deal, so you will be dealt with.)
That is: you will be recompensed for what you do. "اَلدِّينُ" in the language is also habit. The Arabs say: "ما زالَ ذَلِكَ دِينِي" (that has always been my dīn), meaning my habit. The poet said:
تَقُولُ إذا دَرَأْتُ لَها وضِينِي ∗∗∗ أهَذا دِينُهُ أبَدًا ودِينِي
(She says, when I spread out her saddle-girth for her: "Is this forever his habit and mine?")

zajjaj:5-5.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ وإيّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾: the meaning of worship (ʿibāda) in the language is obedience with submission. It is said: "هَذا طَرِيقٌ مُعَبَّدٌ" (this is a beaten road), when it has been made smooth by much treading; and "بَعِيرٌ مُعَبَّدٌ", when a camel has been smeared with tar. So the meaning of "إيّاكَ نَعْبُدُ" is: You alone do we obey with the obedience with which we submit. The position of ﴿إيّاكَ﴾ is accusative, through the verb falling upon it. The position of the kāf in ﴿إيّاكَ﴾ is genitive, through "إيّا" being annexed to it. "إيّا" is a noun for the accusative pronoun, except that it is annexed to the rest of the pronouns, as in: "إيّاكَ ضَرَبْتُ" (you I struck), "إيّاهُ ضَرَبْتُ" (him I struck) and "إيّايَ حَدَّثْتَ" (me you told). If you said "إيّا زَيْدٍ", it would be ugly, because it has been reserved for the pronoun. Yet it has been transmitted from some of the Arabs — al-Khalīl transmitted it: "إذا بَلَغَ الرَّجُلُ السِّتِّينَ فَإيّاهُ وإيّا الشَّوابَّ" (When a man reaches sixty, let him beware of young women).

Whoever says that "إيّاكَ" in its entirety is the noun is told: we have never seen a noun, whether for a pronoun or for an overt noun, that is annexed (in this way); rather, its end changes and what precedes its end remains in one form. The proof of its being annexed is the saying of the Arabs: "إذا بَلَغَ الرَّجُلُ السِّتِّينَ فَإيّاهُ وإيّا الشَّوابَّ يا هَذا", and their treating the hāʾ in "إيّاهُ" as they treat it in "عَصاهُ" (his staff).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَإيّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾: the origin of "نَسْتَعِينُ" is "نَسْتَعْوِنُ", because its meaning is from al-maʿūna and al-ʿawn (help). But the wāw was changed into yāʾ because of the heaviness of the kasra on it: its kasra was transferred to the ʿayn, and the yāʾ remained vowelless, because this is the kind of weak-letter change (iʿlāl) in which one change follows another, as in "أعانَ يُعِينَ" and "أقامَ يُقِيمُ". This is explained in its place in an exhaustive explanation, if Allah wills.

zajjaj:6-6.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿اهْدِنا الصِّراطَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾: its meaning is the clear way. The poet said:
أمِيرُ المُؤْمِنِينَ عَلى صِراطٍ ∗∗∗ إذا اعْوَجَّ المَناهِجُ مُسْتَقِيمُ
(The Commander of the Faithful is on a straight path when the ways have become crooked.)
That is: on a clear road. The meaning of "اِهْدِنا" (guide us), while they are already guided, is: keep us firm upon guidance; just as you say to a man who is standing: "قُمْ لِي حَتّى أعُودَ إلَيْكَ" (stand for me until I come back to you), meaning: remain for me as you are.

zajjaj:7-7.t:
His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿صِراطَ الَّذِينَ أنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ غَيْرِ المَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ ولا الضّالِّينَ﴾: this is a qualification (ṣifa) of His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿الصِّراطَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ [al-Fātiḥa: 6]. In عَلَيْهِمْ you may give the hāʾ ḍamma or kasra; you say: "اَلَّذِينَ أنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ" and "عَلَيْهم" «[Translator's note: the second form is evidently intended as عَلَيْهُمْ, with ḍamma on the hāʾ; the printed text does not show the vowel.]». Most of the readers follow these two dialects. "عَلَيْهِمُو", with wāw, is also permissible. The basic rule for this hāʾ — in your saying "ضَرَبْتُهُو يا فَتى" (I struck him, young man) and "مَرَرْتُ بِهُو يا فَتى" (I passed by him, young man) — is that in connected speech (waṣl) it is pronounced with a wāw; when you pause, you say "ضَرَبْتُهُ" and "مَرَرْتُ بِهِ". Sībawayh held that the wāw was added to the hāʾ in the masculine just as the alif was added in the feminine, in your saying "ضَرَبْتُها" and "مَرَرْتُ بِها", so that masculine and feminine are equal with respect to the addition. The view on this wāw among the followers of Sībawayh and al-Khalīl is that it was added only because of the faintness (khafāʾ) of the hāʾ: the hāʾ comes out of the furthest part of the throat, and the wāw after the hāʾ brings it out of faintness into clarity; that is why it was added. It drops in pause, just as the ḍamma and the kasra drop in your saying "أتانِي زَيْدٌ" (Zayd came to me) and "مَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ" (I passed by Zayd), except that it is a wāw of connection (waṣl), so it is not retained (in pause), lest the connecting element be confused with the original. So when you say "مَرَرْتُ بِهُو يا فَتى", you may, if you wish, say "مَرَرْتُ بِهِي", changing the wāw into yāʾ because of the kasra before it — I mean the bāʾ with kasra «[Translator's note: the text has "الياءَ المُنْكَسِرَةَ" (the yāʾ with kasra); the letter with kasra in بِهِي is the bāʾ, and "الياء" is probably a misprint for "الباء".]».

If someone says: "Between the kasra and the wāw there is the hāʾ", it is replied: the hāʾ is not a solid barrier, so it is as though the kasra were adjacent to the wāw; had the hāʾ been a solid barrier, the wāw would not have been added to it. It has been read: "فَخَسَفْنا بِهِي وبِدارِهِي الأرْضَ" and "بِهُو وبِدارِهُو الأرْضَ" (So We caused the earth to swallow him and his house), from the reading of the people of the Hijaz. If you say "فُلانٌ عَلَيْهِ مالٌ" (So-and-so owes money), you have four options in it: if you wish you give the hāʾ kasra, and if you wish you retain the yāʾ; likewise with ḍamma: if you wish you give the hāʾ ḍamma, and if you wish you retain the wāw. So you say "عَلَيْهِ", "عَلَيْهِي", "عَلَيْهُ" and "عَلَيْهُو مالٌ". As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: "إنْ تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْهِ يَلْهَثْ" (if you attack it, it pants), and His saying: "إلّا ما دُمْتَ عَلَيْهِ قائِمًا" (unless you keep standing over him), the reading is with kasra and without yāʾ in "عَلَيْهِ", and this is the best of these four. One should not read with what is merely permissible, unless a sound transmission establishes it or many of the readers read with it. Whoever says "عَلَيْهُ مالٌ", with ḍamma, the origin in it is "عَلَيْهُو مالٌ", but the wāw was deleted because it is vowelless and the yāʾ is vowelless, and because three homogeneous letters came together, and the ḍamma was left to indicate the wāw. Whoever says "عَلَيْهُو" retains the wāw according to the origin and makes the hāʾ a barrier; this is the weakest of the options, because the hāʾ is not a solid barrier. Whoever says "عَلَيْهِ مالٌ" assumes "عَلَيْهِي مالٌ": he changed the wāw into yāʾ because of the yāʾ before it, then deleted the yāʾ because it is vowelless and the yāʾ before it is vowelless, just as the wāw was changed in his saying "مَرَرْتُ بِهِ يا فَتى". Whoever says "عَلَيْهِي مالٌ", the argument for retaining the yāʾ is like the argument for retaining the wāw. Do you not see that "عَلَيْهِي مالٌ" is better than "عَلَيْهُو مالٌ"? The best of the dialects is what is in the Qur'an, namely His saying "عَلَيْهِ قائِمًا"; next to it in excellence is "عَلَيْهُ مالٌ", with ḍamma; then after this "عَلَيْهِي مالٌ"; then "عَلَيْهُو مالٌ", with the wāw retained, which is the worst of the four.

As for their saying "عَلَيْهم", the basic rule for the hāʾ in what we have described is that it carries a ḍamma, except that the wāw has dropped; the hāʾ is given kasra only because of the yāʾ before it. What precedes the mīm of the pronoun is always with ḍamma, so this ḍamma came only because of the mīm of the pronoun, and it was changed into kasra because of the yāʾ. "عَلَيْهِمْ" and "عَلَيْهم" became frequent in the Qur'an, while "عَلَيْهِمِي" and "عَلَيْهُمُو" did not, only because the ḍamma on the hāʾ of "عَلَيْهم" belongs to the mīm, so it is stronger in being retained. Do you not see that this ḍamma comes before the mīm in everything to which the mīm is attached, such as "عَلَيْكم", "بِكم" and "مِنكم"? In "عَلَيْكم" the form "عَلَيْكِمْ", with kasra on the kāf, is not permissible, because the kāf is a solid barrier between the yāʾ and the mīm, so (its vowel) is not changed into kasra. It has been transmitted from some of the Arabs: "عَلَيْكِمْ" and "بِكِمْ", with kasra on the kāf, but no attention is paid to this transmission. They recited:
وَإنْ قالَ مَوْلاهم عَلى جُلِّ حادِثٍ ∗∗∗ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ رُدُّوا بَعْضَ أحْلامِكِمْ رَدُّوا
(And if their client says, in some great mishap of time: "Bring back some of your forbearance", they bring it back.)
— with kasra on the kāf. This is an anomalous (shādhdh) dialect; the sound transmission is "فَضْلَ أحْلامِكم", and Sībawayh recited it as an anomaly. As for "عَلَيْهِمُو", the basic form of the plural is with a wāw, but the mīm made the wāw dispensable, and the wāw is heavy on their tongues — so much so that among their nouns there is no noun ending in a wāw preceded by a vowel; therefore the wāw was deleted. As for whoever read "عَلَيْهُمُو ولا الضّالِّينَ", it is rare, and one should read only with what is frequent; even though some people have read it so, it is far rarer in the language of the Arabs than the deletion.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿غَيْرِ المَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾: "غَيْرِ" is put in the genitive in two ways. First, as a badal (substitute) for "اَلَّذِينَ", as though He said: "صِراطَ غَيْرِ المَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ" (the path of those other than those who incurred wrath). Second, it is sound for ﴿غَيْرِ المَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ﴾ to be a qualification of "اَلَّذِينَ", even though the basic use of "غَيْرِ" in speech is as a qualification of an indefinite noun. You say: "مَرَرْتُ بِرَجُلٍ غَيْرِكَ" (I passed by a man other than you), and غَيْرُكَ is a qualification of "رَجُلٍ", as though you said: "مَرَرْتُ بِرَجُلٍ آخَرَ" (I passed by another man); and its meaning may also be: "مَرَرْتُ بِرَجُلٍ لَيْسَ بِكَ" (I passed by a man who is not you). It occurs here as a qualification of "اَلَّذِينَ" only because "اَلَّذِينَ" here does not intend specific individuals, so it is equivalent to your saying: "إنِّي لَأمُرُّ بِالرَّجُلِ مِثْلِكَ فَأُكْرِمُهُ" (I pass by a man like you and honour him). It is also permissible to put "غَيْرِ" in the accusative in two ways: as a ḥāl (circumstantial), and as an exception (istithnāʾ), as though you said: "إلّا المَغْضُوبَ عَلَيْهِمْ" (except those who incurred wrath). The proper case of "غَيْرُ" in exception is the accusative when what follows "إلّا" would be accusative. As for the ḥāl, it is as though you said in it: "صِراطَ الَّذِينَ أنْعَمْتَ عَلَيْهِمْ لا مَغْضُوبًا عَلَيْهِمْ" (the path of those You have favoured, not being objects of wrath).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿وَلا الضّالِّينَ﴾: He conjoined "اَلضّالِّينَ" to "اَلْمَغْضُوبِ عَلَيْهِمْ". It was permissible for "لا" to occur in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿وَلا الضّالِّينَ﴾ only because the meaning of "غَيْرِ" includes the meaning of negation. The grammarians allow "أنْتَ زَيْدًا غَيْرُ ضارِبٍ" (you are not one who strikes Zayd), because it is equivalent to your saying "أنْتَ زَيْدًا لا تَضْرِبُ" (you do not strike Zayd), but they do not allow "أنْتَ زَيْدًا مِثْلُ ضارِبٍ", because زَيْدًا belongs to the complement (ṣila) of "ضارِبٍ", so it cannot precede it.

As for what people say after finishing "al-Ḥamd" and the supplication — "آمِينَ" — there are two dialectal forms of it: the Arabs say "أمِينَ" and "آمِينَ". The poet said:
تَباعَدَ عَنِّي فُطْحُلٌ إذْ دَعَوْتُهُ ∗∗∗ أمِينَ فَزادَ اللَّهُ ما بَيْنَنا بُعْدا
(Fuṭḥul drew away from me when I called him — Amen! — so may Allah increase the distance between us.)
The poet also said:
يا رَبِّ لا تَسْلُبَنِّي حُبَّها أبَدًا ∗∗∗ ويَرْحَمُ اللَّهُ عَبْدًا قالَ آمِينا
(O Lord, never take her love away from me; and may Allah have mercy on a servant who says Amen.)
Its meaning is: O Allah, answer. Both are placed in the position of a noun meaning "answering", just as our saying "صَهْ" is placed in the position of "سُكُوتًا" (silence!). Their proper inflection is the pause (indeclinable, without vowel), because they are equivalent to sounds (aṣwāt), since they are not derived from a verb; except that the nūn in them was given fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters. If someone says: "Why was the nūn not given kasra because of the meeting of two vowelless letters?", it is replied: kasra is heavy after yāʾ. Do you not see that "أيْنَ" and "كَيْفَ" were given fatḥa because of the meeting of two vowelless letters, and not kasra, because kasra is heavy after yāʾ?
